div.head: SUMMER AND 'VVINTER.
div.p: SUMMER AND 'VVINTER.

Midsummer morn : the year's young queen Flings showery gold o'er hill and mead, •-:, Her bright train mingles with the green. White cloud-skirts of ethereal brede; The benison of heaven's love lies ,Deep-dwelling in her brave blue eyes. • And life and love breath in her. breath, With fragrance and bird-song made sweet; Her presence kills the worm of death; The children revel round her feet : She comes, God's messenger, to bless Man with immortal happiness. Midwinter noon: the young king-year Comes clothed in panoply of steel; : The furry clouds float, in his rear; Earth rings beneath his armed heel; The pride of life's young vigour ffies, Light-flashing from his keen gray eyes. In glee the lads shout by his side, Their blood-beat pulsing brisk and warm; 4, The stark woods strip their arms, and bide With sinews stiffened for the storm: 1 For Winter comes with strength to bless Man with immortal healthfulness.

, We change, grow old, and sink and die, Fade with the rose, melt with the rime; Nature abides immortally Unchanged in youth, untouched by time; For ciress she flings off green for gray, But her young heart knows no decay. —Good Words.
J. Dow.

I friend should bear his friend's infirmities. In able man shows his spirit by gentle words and re- solute actions. The greatest work which thou canst do is even this— that thou educatest thy child well.—Lather. Fight hard against a hasty temper. Anger will come, but resist it stoutly. A spark may set a house on fire. A fit of passion may give you cause to mourn all the days of your life:— He that revenges knows no rest, The meek possess a peaceful breast. "Where, except in Ireland, would it be possible for a stranger to be accosted, as a writer in the Spectator says be was once accosted by a ragged beggar in Westmeath? Faix, yer 'anuri said the mendicant, "My stomach is sticking to my back; for I'm as empty as a lanthom, wid liever a bit of anything inside o' me but the light of mee ,own conscience." Gondomar, the Spanish ambassador, called upon Lord 'Bacon after his disgrace; and wishing to taunt him in his misfortunes, said, "My Lord, I wish you a merry Easter." "And to you, senor," replied Lord Bacon, 'I wish a good passorer ;" reminding him of his Jewish descent, which was the must cutting retort that could be made to a Spaniard. The porter of a Dublin grocer was brought alp by his master before a magistrate, on a charge which he could not deny. Upon being asked to whom he had sold some chocolate, the pride of Patricic was greatly wounded. "To whom did I sell it?" says Pat; "why, does he think I took the chocolate to sell ?" "Thee, sir," said -the magistrate, " what did you do with it?" "Do with it? Since you must know," gaid he, "I made toy with it." Edward the Confessor, one day lying on his bed, -observed a person (who thought him asleep) take some money out of his casket, with which he went off. He soon returned, and retreated with a secondifooty. On his making a third attempt, "Be as quick as you can," said the King, "for should Hugoline (the King's Chancellor) catch you,you will lose all iyou have got, and be hanged into the bargain." The Chancellor, coming soon after, was greatly concerned at the robbery." "ijegard it not," said the King; "the man who has it winted it More than we." .

TRH bleu:inters CAT.—The cat bath been called a .demestik animile, but-I never could tell whyfore. All there iz domestix about a cat iz, you kant loze one; they are as tuff to laze as a bad reputashun is. Yu may send one out ov the state done up neatly in a mealbag, and the next morning yu will find him along side ov the kitchen stove and' reddy tow be stepped on. They are az sollum as Mczes, but az phull ov the devil as Judas Iskariott, Esq. Thare iz only one thing about a cat that i like, and that iz, they are reasonable : a little money, well put, will go a grate way in cats. Cats are very plentiful in this world lust now. I eetmtedlB from mi boarding house windo, one moon lite rate last summer, and it want the best kind ov a nite foc cats neither.— Josh • NIAGARA FALLS.--SOlllBOllO with a genius for computa- tions has figured up the power of Niagara Falls, and made it cut seven millions horse-power! This immense power, a writer in the Etectrical Engineer thinks, could be employed for electric lighting, and conveyed to -various cities by wires, as suggested or predicted by Sir William Thompson. There are only two great obstacles in the way—the vastness of the scheme and the per- manence of electric lighting. We presume this method of lighting has "come to stay," and farther, that we can look for a more economic transmission of dynamic force by electricity in future. In the tatter matter we think lies more importance for the Niagara project than light- ing. The two, however, go 'together. The electricity, when "conveyed," can be employed for either of these or other purposes.-3f. P. TELE NATURAL HISTORY OF IG/twousße.—The natural history of geniuses iz not the least interesting. A big genius iz generally a phool; he knows how tow do one or two things so much that he aint tit for anything else; he is like a grahound, good for running fast, that's all. 'The most unfortunate thing about having a big genius on hand iz that so many try to imitate them, but they don't generally git any further up than their vices, and thus one big genius suckles a thousand phisols. They don't generally live happy bekause they &tint hilt right , taw fit things as they find them. If I waz a woman, 1.1 -would az soon marry a porcupine as a big genius; they are either as hot as a stove in a skool-house, or as kold and unfeeling as the shoes of a ded omnibus hees. They aint afraid to straddle a hurrykane without 'tinny bridle on, and stick in the spurs; but a mice nibbliag in the wariescut will drive them barheaded into the street.— Josh Bitfias.

Trim STRUGGLE FOR SELF-FOREATION.—WheIthe man has once entered this road, once engaged in the -struggle for self-formation, the ambition of perfection, he soon finds that it is great enough to absorb all his powers; nay, that it calls out in him ehergies of which he never suspected the existence; it opens to him a vista which stretches far beyond the limits of this stage of being; which bridge over the interval between this world and the next, and endows life with a purpose and a meaning which no other pursuit can give it. He has found a rock beneath his feet. He is astonished at the frivolous interests of those around him, their want of earnestness, their superficial hold on life, their apathy to the nobler objects of human pursuit; the levity. monotony, and nonchalance of their conversation, betraying itself even in the tones of their voice. Though he does not seek diversions as they do, he finds that he enjoys life more than they, and can taste its pleasures with a relish which only a pure mind, a clear intention, and a vigilantly watched conscience can bestow. God, and the human destiny to which God has called him, is his presiding thought. The rule of his day is to be always snaking the best of himself. Hence his security—the confidence with which he steps from his retirement into the world. To use the image of St. Francis de Sale, he handles the things of this world as an infant reaches forward to gather flowers with one hand, while with the other it grasps tight the hand of its father—From Sermons by Mark Patlison. THE BrrEn Brs—Some boys boardea with a teacher in Scotland, whose house was not far from a country churchyard. They determined to alarm the old grave- digger, who was in the habit of reaching his cottage, often late at night, by a short cut through the burying ground. One boy named Warren, who was especially mischievous, and had often teased old Andrew, dressed himself up in a white sheet, and with his companions hid behind the graves. After waiting patiently, but not without some anxiety and fear, for Andrew, he was at last seen approaching the memorial stone behind which Warren was ensconced. Soon a number of low moans were heard coming from amongst the graves. " Ah, keep us a' !" exclaimed Andrew. "What's that r And as he approached slowly and cautiously towards the tombstone a white figure arose, and got taller and taller before his eyes. "What's this 2" asked Andrew, with a voice which seemed to tremble with fear, although if anyone bad seen how he grasped his stick, he would not have seen his hand tremble. "It's the resurrection!" exclaimed the rreverent Bully Warren. "The resurrection!" replied Andrew. " May I tak' the leeberty o' askin'," he con- tinued, slowly approaching the ghost, "if it's the general ane, or are ye list takin' a quiet daunder by zersel'?" So saying, Andrew rushed at the ghost, and seizing it, while a number of other smaller and darker ghosts rose end ran off in terror to the schoolhouse, he exclaimed: " Come awe' wi' me! I think I surely haena' buried ye deep eneuch, when ye can rise so easy. But I hae dug a fine deep grave this morning, an' I'll pit ye in't, and cover ye up wi' sae muckle yirth that my word yell no get oet for anither daunder." So saying, Andrew, by way of carrying out his threats, dragged Master Bully Warren toward a newly-made grave. The boy's horror illay be imagined, as Andrew was too powerful to permit a his escape. He assailed the old man with agonised petitions for mercy, for he was a great coward. "I'm not a ghost! Oh, Andrew, I'm Peter Warren I Andrew! Andrew! don't bury me I'll never again annoy you! Oh—o-o-o-o 1" Andrew, after he had administered what he considered due punishment, let Warren off with the admonition: "Never daur tae speak o' gude things in yen Way. Never play at ghaists again, or leevin' folk like me may grup you, an' tnak' a ghaist o' ye. Aff wi' ye!" FOR ROUGH, BED. RAINEALL.—A rain that amounts to one inch in depth equals 100 tons on each acre of ground. This amount of water suffices for two persons for one year. The rainfall in England is about 36 inches annually, and is 180 times as much as the population requires for the ordinary uses of life. Another artistic find has been made in the City. Re- cent researches in the cellars beneath the old courts of law in the Guildhall have brought to light three statues which formerly stood in front of Guildhall Chapel. They are life-size representations of Edward VL, Charles L and his consort, Queen Henrietta Maria. They are said to be of the date of the Great Fire of London, and are all well preserved. In San Francisco, where the gradients are as steep as any yet attempted on lines for regular circulating traffic, the breaks are not placed on the wheels but on the rails. They consist of bars of wood, two to three feet long, that can be jammed down between the wheels with fotce enough to lift a carriage from the ways, wheels and all. There is no doubt a gain resulting from such breaks, in avoiding wear upon the wheels. In short, the right place to apply any break would seem to be on the ways instead of the wheels. TREASURE TROVE.—A few days ago, while some'work- men were pulling down an old building in the town of Svenborg, on the island of Fiinen, they came ;upon a valuable treasure, which included 10 bars of very fine silver and 3,774 silver and gold coins, all dating from the reign of the Danish Kin°. Eric of Pomerania (Am. 1396- 1412). The whole lay together buried in the basement close to the foundation. It is singular that a tradition. of centuries pointed to this house as a place where trea- sure had been buried, and the owner when selling it a shorttime since expressly reserved the ownership of any treasure that might be foundon the premises. FISHES AS NEST BUILDERS.—Amongst the fishes, it is by no means unusual to find nest builders. The case of the familiar sticklebacks, which build nests for the re- ception of the eggs, has already been noticed in these pages. Here the display of anxiety for the developing young isof the most marked 'character; It is the male stickleback which keeps watch and ward over the off- spring. He is a pugnacious being, keeping all intruders at a distance. Even the mother fish is not allowed to approach the nest; the unusual practice of forbidding the mother being unfortunately clearly justifiable on the ground of her unnatural and cannibal-like propensity ; to feed upon the •eggs. Hence the faithful little male! stickleback performs the duties of guardian and nurse; with great fidelity; constantly swimming round and round the nest, and menacing all datruders.—Charabers's journal. .

THE PUNISTMENT Os CrimmiEN.—One thing is certain, and that is that there is among ,ehildren ,an !infinite variety of physique and temperament, and that one child can endure without harm what would do serious injury to another. It is desirable, therefore, either that the more delicate little ones shall not 'be punshed at all, or that some penalty shall be found which can be ad- ministered to them without detriment to their :health. There are surely other ways of making,a child realise:the enormity of its conduct than personal chastisement. Probably, if certain teachers knew their business better, there would be -fewer occasions for punishing young people; and certainly the correction ought to be care- fully adapted to theaaffence and the offender. The prob- lem is, however, 'rather for parents than for teachers. Parents ought to know the constitutionof their children, and should keep a Close watchon what goes on at school: If the youngsters are not strong, the teacher should be told so, and no doubt they would not be; tasked or punished beyond their eapacity.—Lancet. AFRICAN TRAVEL.—At the meeting of the Royal Geo- , graphical Society, on the 30th inst., Mr. Walter Montagu Kerr will read a paper upon his recent journey in Africa in whieh were two noteworthy features. Mr.lierr is the first traveller who, so far as in known, has reached the:Lake regions from the south. He also has the distinction of having perforibed the journey alone, solely depending upon the natives he met for aid and guidance. In the latter respect the journey is of more than ordinary in- terest, for it showe that exploration can be effected without the help of large bodies of carriers and guides, such as have been thought necessarily associated in enter- prises of a like nature. Mr. Kerr's journey carried him j through the disputed lands lying on the northern fron- tier of our Cape dominions. Thence he travelled through Matabele and Mashona lands and the country of.s. little- known people named Makorikoti. After crossing the Zambesi he was subjected to many hardships. He found ; the mission station of Livingstonia deserted. Here, and upon the shores of Lake Nyassa, Mr. Kerr wandered alone till he found a French exploring party. Accom- panied by the chief of the party, Lieutenant Giraud, he finally reached the coast THE NEWLY-FOUND STATUE or BAtORDSUq RonE.—A Naples correspondent writes :—" The chalky incrusta- tion which covered the bronze statue lately found in the bed of the Tiber has been removed, and the admirable modelling of the statue has thus been fully revealed. It is one of the most beautiful works of the kind, and, with the exception of some damage to the legs and left hand, is in a capital state of preservation. The statue, about six feet high, is doubtless that of the youthful , Bacchus. In the left hand is the usual staff, while the right probably held a drinking-cup, in the attitude so often seen in pictures of the god at Pompeii. The soft and feminine form, the ivy wreath on the head, the luxu- riously waving hair, which is modelled in the manner of the hair of Apollo, are other proofs that the statue was meant for Bacchus. It seems to belong to the first cen- tury of the Roman Empire, when Rome was illuminated by the last rays of Greek art. The lines'and surfaces of the statue in all the uninjured parts are as fresh and pure as if the work had just left the master's hand. The , figure was only half-buried, head downwards, in the bed of the river, so that the action of the water has rough- ened the lower parts. The eyes inserted are of ivory, and give extraordinary vitality to the expression." ROLLED SCREWS.—The screw threads are formed by rolling the blanks between two metallic surfaces, both cut so as to form dies, which produce the thread. The blanks are formed in a separate machine, and are then placed, several hundred at a time, in a hopper in which works a lifter having a vertical motion. At each dip the lifter fishes up out of the mass of blanks a number, which arrange themselves head upwards in a groove along which they are automatically carried to the forming por- tion of the machine. This consists of a revolving circu- lar die, between which and a stationary section the blanks are carried forward, their revolution under compression producing the thread which is raised on the blank., This is effected without cutting or waste, and, in the machine we saw operated, at the rate of a gross, or 144 screws, per minute. The screw thus formed is found to possess many advantages over the ordinary screw with the cut thread. These advantages, besides being apparent on the face of it, are admitted by experts who have thoroughly tested the Harvey screw. In the first place it has a true gimlet point, drawing the screw into the wood in a straight course, and doing away almost en- tirely with the use of the gimlet. The thread is found to , be much stronger, the metal being rolled up and com- pressed. In the ordinary screw at present in use the fibre is Cut, arid thereby weakoned. Another :point of great value is that the neck of the Harvey screw is of I smaller diameter than the thread, whereas, in the ordi- nary screw the neck is larger than the thread, necessi- tating in hard wood the use of two gimlets to avoid splitting.—Mecitanica/ Progress.

ftik ' THE EXAMIN ' Labour, like eveiry other commodity that is bought try, and sold, is subject to the law of supply and demand. for The less the supply in proportion to the demand, the greater will be its price. Therefore, with a given supply of labour, every cause that tends to diminish the de- mand just as certainly tends to diminish the price at which it is to be sold. Dr. John Hunter, the eminent surgeon, adopted a rule which may be recommended to aIL When a friend asked him how he had been able to accomplish so much in the way of study and discovery in his busy life, be answered, ‘llly rule is deliberately to consider, before I commence, whether the work is practicable. If it be not practicable, Ido not attempt it. If it be practicable. I can accomplish it if I give sufficient pains to it; and, having begun, I never stop until the thing is done. To this rule I owe all my success in life." AGE OF THE EARTH.—The age of the earth is estimated from the increment on temperature as the crust is pene- trated. The data is not precise, and is aot so claimed, but from the above and other evidences, Sir William Thompson thinks the earth to be at least 100,000,000 years old, since it became crusted over. The increase of temperature towards the centre diminishes with time and the thickness of the crust. The increase of tem- perature in the low levels of mines furnishes practical evidence of the change as we penetrate the earth. THE ART OF Woaxixo.—Watch a good workman. He is never in a hurry; he never works fast; he seldom gets tired, and when he is tired, he stops. The great art of working is not to go beyond your pace. Every good horse has its pace, and in that pace he will do ten miles with pleasure, and come in fresh. Urge him beyond his pace, or fret him with alternate fast and slow, he will show signs of fatigue, and end his day exhausted. One test whether we are working right or wrong is our enjoyment of our work, or our want of enjoyment. The person who is working calmly and doing his best takes pleasure in his work.

According to the latest statistics, the Scotch are the tallest and heaviest. In height the Scotch first (68.61 in. the Irish second (67.90 in. the English third (67.361 n. and the Welsh last (66.66 in. the average of the whole being 67.661 n. In weight the Scotch take the first place (165.31 b. the Welsh second (158.31 b. the English third (1551 b. and the Irish fourth (154-11 b. the average of the whole being 158.21 b. Thus the Scotch are the tallest and heaviest. the English take the third place in both tables, while the position of the Welsh and Irish is reversed—the Irish, occupying second place in stature, come last in weight; and the Welsh, though lowest in stature, stand second in weight. BIOLOGY IN THE MEDICAL CURRICULLIM.—In :opening the new biological laboratory in the University College of North Wales, Professor Michael Foster made some well- timed observations on the true place of biology in medi- cal education. Physiology, he truly said, formed the key of the position in medicine. It dealt with the natural action of processes whose perverted state was embraced by the term pathology. While thus related on the one hind with actual disease and its treatment, it required for the complete and ready mastery of its details some knowledge of the forms and functions which are treated of in biological science. There is a tendency in our day to make rather too little of botany and zoology in the studies of the medical curriculum, and to give, perhaps, undue prominence to physics. The need of acquiring, within a limited time, is knowledge of many -subjects, and a deep and practical acquaintance with those which are specially professional, renders it difficult to allot to the introductory studies their due share of attention. It should be possible, nevertheless, to allow to each of the j sciences we have named a separate entity. They would thus receive a measure of justice proportionate to 'their bearing on other subjects, which could hardly be ex- pected' if they were mere adjuncts of anatomy and material medics on the one hand, or of ehemistry on the other. The formation of a laboratory for biological -study' is a feature of note in the new College of Wales. It is an earnest that practice is`not to be forgotten in theory, and will, WS hope, serve as an example in the formation of the other scientific and medical classes.—Loacet. WIND VELOCITY OF OVER A HUNDRED MILES AN Hone.— Many interesting observations were made at the Ben Nevis Observatory during the violent storm which pre- vailed about the end of last month, and which was felt over many parts of the kingdom. The first indications of the storm were observed on Ben Nevis about four o'clock on the afternoon of Tuesday, the 29th of Sept., when the barometer began to fall—slowly at first, after- wards more 'rapidly; and the wind, which had been westerly, began to back, at the same time increasing in force. After midnight the barometer fell at the rate of over 1-10 in, per hour, and between four and five o'clock on Wednesday morning a fall of nearly 2401 n. was re- corded.* At three o'clock a.m. the wind was south- easterly, blowing half a gale. Fortunately, the thaw which took place on Tuesday had hardened the surface of the snow, so that there was very little drift, the soft snow being cleared at once. By four o'clock the wind was blowing a full gale—force, 9 on the Beaufort scale— and it continued to increase in strength :te force 10 at five o'clock, the maximum being reached about six o'clock, when for a short time observations became almost impossible,the force at that hour being 11,1 which represents is velocity of over 100 miles an hour. A thaw then set in, the wind veering to southerly, and diminish- ing greatly in force. Subsequently the barometer rose on the whole, but rather unsteadily. "'Fortunately no damage was done during the continuance of the storm, either to the observatory or to Mr. Whyte's hotel, ex- cept that the chimney of the latter was blown down. The work of the observatory was carried on as usual, none of the observations being interrupted. At one time during the storm the barometer had fallen at Stor- noway below 28'8in.—Engineering. WHY LAW Is AN EXPERSIVE Luxtrny. Litigation must always be a somewhat expensive luxury, though it might be very much cheaper than it is; and,that it is so expensive is, to some extent, the suitor's own fault. If th*ublic will persist in employing only leading stars of the first magnitude they must bear the cost, and, moreover., run the risk of their not shining just when their light is most needed. Aided and abetted by ' solicitors, they deliberately throw all the work into the hands of a favoured few, and thus run up the foes of I fashionable counsel. And so long as solicitors think they can evade responsibility by employing only those with great names it is difficult to see how this can be avoided, except by making solicitors responsible for their counsel's absence. If solicitors were liable to their clients, and counsel to the solicitors who employ them„,iolicitors would not be so ready to take briefs to those already over- whelmed with work, and counsel would be more chary about accepting work they could not properly attend to. This would, we admit, be but a partial remedy ; but it would do something to disperse work, and thus benefit both the bar and the public. We should be sorry for some reasons to see the fees of counsel changed from an honorarium into a quantum 2ntruit ; but we confess we see no other means by which the evil is to be mitigated. . . . It never seems to strike the public mind that there can be destitution at the Bar, but such does a un- doubtedly exist; and but for the fact that so many barris- ters have private incomes it would be very widespread. Instances are not unknown of men working and wait- ing, living on pauper's fare, and shutting themselves out from society into which they could not afford to] enter, till disappointment and starvation had done their work, and ended a blighted existence and a hopeless struggle. Had Dickens turned his genius in is different direction, and depicted the threadbare counsel instead of:the slip- shod suitor, the would have found an equally pitiful, but far more werthy, subject for his romance. Those, of course, are extreme cases. But when we remember that a man may think himself lucky if, after 10 orls years' I hard and profitless labour, he makes £5OO a year, and that even this is precarious and liable to be determined ! by illness or an accident, when we remember that year ! by year he sees the bread taken out of his mouth by legislation, we may fairly conclude that no body of men is so hard-working or so ill-paid as the rank and file of the junior Bat—From "Forensic Facts and Fallacies" (Macmillan and Co.) VULGAR BELIEFS IN THE MONITIONS OF TUB STARS.— Eclipses, comets, and conjunctions of the superior planets, play a great part in the state astrology. Some j well-authenticated cases of success in this department ! are on record. One astrologer, by name Landino, ac- cording to Villari, drew the horoscope of religion, and ; predicted, from a conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn that ' on the 25th November, 1484, a great reformation of the Christian religion would take place; and it is singular that Luther was born in the very month of November of 1483 or 1484—some doubt existing as to the year. Tycho Brahe predicted, from the comet of 1577, that in the north of Finland there would be born a prince, who should lay waste Germany, and vanish in 1632. Now, Gustavus Adolphus, it is well known, was born in:Fin- land, overran ',Germany, and died in 1632. It is also very singular that during the very worst period of the late troubles in Ireland, Saturn would have been !pass- ing through Taurus, a sign which astrologers say rules Ireland, and prior to the passing of the Land Act, Jupiter and Venus should have been in conjunction with Saturn in the same reign. Also, just before the assassination of President Garfield two Comets first seen in the United States—appeared in right ascension, corresponding to Gemini, a sign, again, said by astro- logers to rule the United States. Now, it is an old jastrological doctrine that a comet, visible to the naked eye, appearing in the ruling sign of a country, portends the violent dqath of the chief ruler. There is.no doubt that it is because of chance coincidence of this sort that astrology maintained its place for such a long period of time, and that even at the present day many, otherwise well educated people, are led to think "there is some- thing in it." Flamsteed, the Astronomer Royal of that day, it is said, astrologically "elected" the favourable time for the foundation of Greenwich Observatory. A great deal too much is made of the effects of scientific inquiry in putting down divinatory and other supersti- tions, The fact is very few people have the ability to thoroughly grasp scientific truth_ Tbej real truth why we at the present day in the West of Europe have little to do with astrologers and fortune tellers is because life amongst us has become fairly certain in its general cir- cumstances. Great epidemics are comparatively rare; physical catastrophes, like earthquakes, are still more rare; against common uncertainties of various sorts we have all kinds of systems of insurance; and last, but not least, we must not forget the efficacy of law, and the general respect there is for it. Reverse all these circum- stances, gg back not much more than two centuries ago, and we reach a state of society, even in our own coun-

A niurderer, after execution, was put in his coffin and delivered over for burial. For some purpose of identification the coffin was opened, and it was found the man had been buried alive. These kinds of horrors are always taken hold of by persons who would abolish capital punish- ment; but they only point to this, that the hang- man must he paid by the State, and be responsible for' his work. In America there is agitation to find some substitute for hanging, and we shall probably see the gnillotine adopted there, and then at second hand introduced here.

The electric light is making way in London by a new and most convenient channel. I was dining last night at a friend's house and observed that the dining table was illuminated by the electric light, whilst other rooms in the house had the ordinary gas light. I inquired 'how this came to pass, and learned that the lights on the table were temporarily fixed. The electricity is supplied by accumulators, which are brought into the house, placed under the table, connection formed along the line of the can- delebra, and there is the electric light as complete and as beautiful as if, like some magnates in Lon- don—such as Lord Randolph Churchill, one of the first to burn the electric light—there were an engine on the premises and an engineer in charge. 'The next morning the men came and took away the accumulators and the lamps, and things revert to their old style till the next dinner party. The charge for the whole business is, I believe, very reasonable, and nothing could be more convenient. The men of Mid-Lothian are already provided with a candidate in the event, which it is hoped is far off, of Mr. Gladstone's retirement from the repre- sentation of the county. The gentleman is Mr. Gibson Carmichael, son of a well-known Scotch , baronet and large landowner, partly in Mid-Lothian and partly in Peeblesshire. Amocgst the group of cheerful young men who voluntarily gave up their time to advancing the prospects of Mr. Gladstone, Mr. Carmichael is known as "Mr. Gladstone's under- study." Perhaps I should explain for little boys -who do not go to the theatre that all great actors and actresses of the London theatres have in attend- ance a member of the company prepared at a moment's notice to take their place, supposing they are incapacitated by sudden illness. He or she is called "an under-studier." Hence the applicability to Mr. Carmichael. At one of the meetings some one attempted to improve upon this, alluding to Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Carmichael as "the Young Oba- diah and the Old Obadiah." The next speaker promptly retorted that he did not see any similarity between the two Obadiahs of the song and Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Carmichael. But he admitted that when he heard Mr. Dalrymple speak he was inclined to chant the refrain of the song, "I am dry, lam dry." Mr. Dalrymple was Mr. Gladstone's op- ponent, a fact which it may be well to mention, as he was so entirely an obscurity that few knew his name.

Whilst hunting with Lord Middleton's hounds, near Mal.. ton, on Wednesday, Dr. Hartley's horse made a false leap at a fence and fell with the rider beneath. Dr. Hartley was so badly injured that he died shortly after being picked up. The agitation in the Northern and Midlind coal trade for an advance of wages has collapsed. The defection of the South Yorkshire miners was announced a few days ago, and now we learn that throughout Lancashire the men are with- drawing their notices.

If you have an enemy, act kindly to him, and make him your friend. You may not win him over at once, but try again. Let one kindness be followed by another, till you have accomplished your end. By little and little great things are accomplished:— Water falling day by day • Wears the hardest rock away. And so repeated kindness will soften a heart of stone. Lady Wallace, overtaking a gentleman of her acquain- tance who was walking along in a thoughtful mood, slapped him on the hack, and cried out, "Pray, sir, can you tell me how old I am ?" "Madam,'. replied he, turning round, "I cannot be very exact, but you cer- tainly have not arrived at years of discretion." "Susan," said an Irish footman to his fellow-servant, "what are the bells ringing for again?" "In honour of the Duke of York's birthday, Mr. Murphy." "Be aisy, now," rejoined the Hibernian, "none of your blarney. Sure, 'twits the Prince Regent's on Tuesday, and how can it be his brother's to-day, unless, indeed, they. are twins."

, --- RUGBY RULES. SANKEY 2ND T. ROVERS 25D.—Played on Saturday on the ground of the latter' and resulted in a victory for the visitors by one try, one disputed try, and two minors to two minors. RUNCORN OLD BOYS y. WESTON Ti 0' SHANTERS.— The representative teams of these clubs met on the Shan- ters' field, Weston, on Saturday, the game ending in draw in favour of the Shanters by four minor points to nil. RUNCORN WATERLILIES V. TAM O'SHANTERS.—PIayed on Saturday on the former's ground, and ended in favour of the Shanters by one try, four minor points. The game was hardly contested throughout, both teams playing well. HA.LERANK v. WIDNES TRITE BLUES.—These two clubs met for the first time this seasen on the ground of the for- mer. The game resulted in favour of Halebank by one try to two minors. Blues one disputed goal and three minors. Halebank : Back, D. Barker; three-quarters, Peters, Bro- derick, Trascott ; half-back, Longton Hartles ; forwards, G. Lewis (captain), J. Lewis, A. dartland. R. Baxter, Brady, Royle, Gill. Bevan, H. White. WARRINGTON RANGERS V. PENKETEL—This match was played on the ground of the latter on Saturday. The home team was very strong, whilst the visitors were weak. The Rangers kicked off against both wind and hill. When no side was called it left the visitors winners by one try and 2 touch in goals to 1 dead ball for the home team. Teams— Rangers: Full back, Hassell; three•quarters, Minshull, Cook, and Mather; half backs, J. Boyle and Robinson (cap- tain) ; forwards, Edwards, Hill, Buckley, Shaw, Foster, Holt, Hughes, Bate, and Boyle. Penketh : Fall back, Forden ; three-quarters, Fairhurst. Dumville, and Hooper; half backs, Whittle and F. Samson; forwards Green, Tongue, Tomlinson, Ainsworth, Wilkinson, Shave, J. Sam- sona, Appleton, and Routledge. ST. PALM'S F.C. v. WARRINGTON ROVERS (SECOND).— This match was played on Saturday, on the ground of the latter. Pow-nail won the toss for the visitors, and elected to . play against the wind. The first half was very hard on both sides only minors being registered. At half time the score stood—St. Paul's, 3 minors, to Rovers 2 minors. The , second half was all in favour of the visitors. The good ' combined play of the forwards and the passing of the half ; backs enabled Speakman to kick three goals in less than ten minutes. Emson also gained for the visitors a try from a • good dribble. Eventually" time" was called, leaving St. 1 Paul's the victors by 3 goals, 1 try, and 3 minors, to 2 r minors. Litton, Jones. and Hordern played well for the ; losers. Tema :--St. Paul's : Full back, C. Onions; three- quarter backs, Emson, Allford, and Speakman ; half backs, , A. Oxley and J. Warburton ; forwards, Marriott, Jolley, ' W. Oxley, J. Seed, W. Hosker, W. Praeger, J. Pownall ' (captain), Roughley, and Berry. Rovers: Full back, E. Hackett ; three-quarter backs, Ihsllian, Hordern, and Lit- ' ton ; half backs, F. Jones and J. Fair ; forwards, Flet- cher, J. Jones, W. Jones, Spinks, Barker, Smith, Woods, • and Dumbell. SANKEY v. WIDENS EXCELSIORS.—The return match t between these clubs was played at Sankey on Saturday. , Owing to the rainy weather the ground was in a wretched . condition. Both teams appeared on the field about 3 30. 3 The visiting captain won the toss, and elected to play ; with the wind and ground in his favour. The ball being started, the visitors followed up, and the home team were forced to save after about a minute from the start. From the drop out the borne forwards rushed the ball up the field, but Locke saved. A scrimmage was formed, when Woolley gained possession, and was looking dangerous when be was pushed into touch. From the line-up the ball was passed to Barton, who, seeing he was surrounded by the ' "enemy," took a drop at goal, but the ball was charged down. The visitors again took the ball to the opposite end of the field, and the home team were forced to save. After the drop-out the home forwards came with a combined dribble, and Barton, picking up smartly, ran in and secured a try. The visitors made an appeal for off•side, but the referee decided against it. The kick at goal was a failure. Up to half-time the ball was kept in mid-field, but on the change of earls the home team severely pressed their op- ponents, forcing them to save three times in rapid succession. Another try was scored for the home team, but was disal- lowed. Up to call of time nothing more was scored on either side, leaving the home team the winners by two tries (one disputed) and four minor points to two minor points. Mr. R. Whitfield acted as umpire for the home team, and Mr. Fair. Turner (of the Warrington Football Club), as referee.

WARRINGTON.V. Bovros.—Played at Bolton on Saturday. Warrington were without the services of Buxton, Barnes, Jolley, and Gilbert, backs, Fair Turner, Speakman, Dillon, and Rigby, forwards, the team being made up of 13 men from the "A team." Eagan and Rirnmer's services also being se- cured at Newton. It was decided, owing to the stormy weather, to play 20 minutes each way, and Warren for War- rington winning the toss, elected to play with the wind. The ball being started by Bolton, was well returned, and from a scrimmage inside the home 25 flag Warren neatly passed to Boardman, who, eluding the home backs, gained a try, the place being taken by Frank Turner, resulting in no goal. The leather being again put in motion, the Warring• ton forwards dribbled the ball over the borne line, a touch- down being recorded. The ball being again started, Warren emerged from a scrimmage formed in mid-field, and was not , brought down until a few yards off the home line, the ball ' being dribbled over; a minor resulted. Shortly afterwards the Bolton territory was again invaded, and Boardman run- ning to within a few yards of the home line, passed neatly to Nevins, who laded the second try for Warrington, Frisk Turner taking the place, who failed to add the major point. At the call of half-time, the visitors by combined driblelee had added 3 more minor points to their score. On resumption of play, the Warrington forwards quickly worked the ball to the home goal, another minor point be- ing registered. After some give and take play, from a serimmage formed in the Bolton 25, Boardman again se- cured the leather and crossed the home line, no goal result- ing, Yellowing the kick out, the Warrington forwards al- ways having the best of the backs quickly had the ball in front of the home goal, and Warren passing to Massey, the lattew essayed a drop at goal, a minor resulting. Scrim- mages were again indulged in in the home territory, and Warren again passing to Massey, the latter had a clear run In, Rimmer taking the place kick failed to put the ball over the bar. Time being shortly afterwards called, Warrington were left the winners by 4 tries and 7 minors to nil. For the winners Warren and Boardman were the pick of the backs and kshton and Povey forwards, the two latter fre- quently coming through the packs with the ball at their Lova—Teams: Warrington—Back. Hewitt; three-quarter backs, Maseey, Boardman, and Rimmer ; half-backs, War- ren and Eagan; forwards, H. Boardman, Haugh, Davies, Ashton, Povey, Elayee, Forster, Nevins, Savage; umpire, T. Barnes. Bolton—Back, "Staton " three-quarter backs, Ban. croft, Mangnall, and Litter, halt-backs, Johnson and Boon ;1 forwards, Tristram, Kershaw, Bentley, Hopper, Walker, Rutter, Lomax, Farnworth, and another. Runcorn; v. Setae—A large amount of interest was taken in the meeting of the above teams at Runcorn on Saturday, and though the weather was miserable, a large gathering of spectators watched a good game, which the home team won by one goal, two tries, three minor points, I to Sale nothing. Lewis kicked off from centre, when the play located in the Sale territory, and after some loose play Wright picked up and forced a way through his opponents over the line, scoring the first try, the kick at goal failing.' Following the drop out, E. Lings and Dzinkwater put in some good work, Joule neutralising by a short dribble, and Speakman afterwards scoring a minor point from a drop at goal. Play was again restarted, but the vieitora were kept mostly in their half during the remainder of the game. After crossing over, Lings restarted, and W. Hughes and Holland took the ball towards the Sale quarter. Paine sent the ball back to Woods, who returned it again. Another effert by Speakman resulted in a dead ball. Lunt replied to Hunt's drop out, and by the smart following up of the home forwards, headed by Barns, Cox, and Broady. Cox crossed the line close to the posts, Woods kicking a goal. After a start had again been made from centre, the ball falling amongst the forwards the borne front rank took on the ball near the Sale line, where Speakman was only held on the line, the scrimmage ending in Broughton touching down. Lunt, in reply to the drop into play, carried the ball into the Sale half, and H. Hughes, running across, gave the ball back to Johnson, who throughout had played a capital defensive game, but he was pushed into touch. The ball was carried on up to the Sale line, when Barns grounded it over, the kick at goal failing. From this to the close of the game the visitors were pressed, the match ending as indicated above. For Sale, Paine, Broughton, and Drinkwater behind the pack, and E. Lings T. Liege Hunt, and Hardy forward did a lot of hard work'. Of the home team, Speakman played well behind, being well sup- ported by his colleagues of the back division, and among the forwards Broady, Cox, Cams, Hughes, and Huff:land showed well. The following were the teams :—Sale: J. W. Paine, back ; F. E. Holt, J. Cookson, and W. Greenlaugh, three-quarter backs ; S. Broughton and F'. Drinkwater, half-back,- E. Lings, T. Lingo, E. W. Hunt, J. W. Wil- kinson, W. Hardy, J. Snowball, J. Abrams, T. Whinyates, and W. Dunbavand, forwards. Runcorn : T. Woods, tack ; E. Lunt, H. C. Speakman, and T. Johnson, three•quarter backs ;H. Hughes and W. Antrobus half-backs; W. , Wright, W. Hughes, J. Lewis, J. Barns, J. Holland, W. IL Broady, J. Gattey, W. Cox, and F. G. Joule, forwards. Referee. Mr. F. T. Parry, Liverpool. ASSOCIATION RULES., ST. HELENS AMATEURS V. WIDNES ASSOCIATION.—The first encounter with the two above clubs took place at Dun- riding-lane, on Saturday, in very unpleasant weather, and a very quiet game resulted in a victory for the Amateurs by three goals to love.

WIGAN CUP TIE,--HAYDOCK v. A DLINGTON.—These teams met limbo second round of the competition for the Wigan and District Challenge Cop on Monday afternoon. The tie was played at Adlington, and the home team won by seven goals to five. When time was called the score stood five goals each, but in the extra half hour which was played the Adlington team scored two more goals, and thus won.

DESPERATE FIGHTING—PIROT TAKEe GARIANS.—AN ARMISTICE CONCLUDe,D. SOPHIA, FRIDAY.—The battle at Pirot commenced this morning at about seven o'clock. Tire Servians occupied fortified positions on the heights to the right and left of the town, their lines extending in the direction of Nisch, Four Servian divisions were brought into action, the Bul- garians attacking in three columns. After a sanguinary engagement the Servians abandoned their position on the left. The ight was prolonged on the right, but eventually the Bulgarians, charging the enemy with the bayonet, forced them to retire in disorder. Pirot is now occupied by the Bulgarian troops. who have also advanced for a distance of several kilometres beyond the town. The fighting was Of a meet desperate character, the Servians and Bulgarians bayonetting each other in the streets. i SOPHIA., SITURDAY.—Haying taken into consideration 1 the collective representations made by the Great Powers, , and the declaration of Count Khevenleueller, wbo, in the i name of the Emperor of Austria, informed his Highness that should the Bulgarian troops advance another kilometre on Servian territory Austrian troops would cross the Servian frontier, and the Bulgarians would then have to meet Aus- trian instead of Servian troops, and also that the Prince's military honour was saved and. his reputation assured by the eapture of Picot, Prince Alexander to-day issued orders to the Bulgarian Generals to cease hostilities and enter into . negotiations for an agreemest regarding the terms of an armistice between the two countries. lines, SATURDAY.—Yesterday, the Bulgarians made a sortie from Widdin and attacked the entire line of the be- sieging force. The fighting was of an obstinate character, the combatants finally crossing Bayonets. The Bulgarians , were drivenback, and forced to retire into the fortress. The , Bulgarian prisoners declare that the losses on their side • were excessively heavy. Bulgarian soldiers are giving themselves up in small groups. 1 BELGRADE, SATURDAY.—Through the intermediary of L Count Khevenhueller, the Austrian Mieister, an armistice e was concluded at half-past three this afternoon,between Ser- Via, and Bulgaria, both of the belligerents remaining in , their present positions. 19 [bona., SUNDAY.—Notwithstanding the armistice the Sec- , vian advanced posts this 'morning 'attacked the Bulgarian • Positions at Aria Palanka, on the Danube. The Bulgarian IGovernment has notified this violation of the armistrce to the representatives of the Great Powers. . RusTCHVE, SUNDAY.—Yesterday aTe Deum of thanks- ':- giving for the capture of Pirot by the Bulgarian army was sung in the Cathedral here. ~, CONSTANTINOPLE, SUNDAY.—It is believed that the armis- ' eine concluded between Servia and Bulgaria will greatly facilitate the task of the Conference. ' BEDGRADE, MONDAY.—An eye-witness of the fighting at Pirot states that after the Bulgarians bad taken the town at nightfall, two thousand Servian cavalry fell upon there and ~, tut them to pieces, the streets being strewn with dead and - wounded, and running with blood. The Bulgarians then , left the town, but returned to the attack later on in in- , Creased numbers. The heights held by the Servians were defended with 20 guns, both on the right and left. During ' the struggle two Bulgarian battalions were surrounded by Servians, and declining to surrender, were decimated by ; the artillery fire. Finally. the Bulgarians forced the Ser. 'flans to abandon the heights, hut only after suffering ter- rible loses. , BRUSSELS, SUNDAY.—The Ilrord accuses England ef be- ing the cause of the delay in the peaceful settlement of the . Balkan question. RUSSIAN APPROVAL OF BULGARIA. SOFIA, MONDA.Y.—Everything quiet. All tile ministers have gene to Pirot to confer with Prince Alexander. Sr. PETERSEURCI, TUESDAY. The following imherial Order has been issued :—Although deeply afflicted by the . fratricidal war in Eastern Europe, the Emperor coneiders ;- the determination, abnegation, perseverance, and love of ' order displayed by the Bulgarian and Rournelian troops to ' be worthy of high prais2, mindful of the fact that these ' t,rooes had their military qualities and heroic Inertial spirit imparted to them by the judgment and self-sacrificing spirit of Russian officers The Emperor thanks Prince Lent, en- oene, and assures of his favour all Russian officers who have served in Bulgaria or Routnelia. SERVIAN PROPOSALS REJECTED BY BULGARIA. SOFIA, WEDNESDAY, 430 .P.ll.—The Servian Envoy Charged by King Milan to treat with Prince Alexander concerning the conditions of the armistice has proposed tha : evacuation by both belligerents of the positions occupied by . theire. armies on each others territory, and the prolongation °I the suspension of hostilities until Jan aary 1. The pro- - Posal hes , Servia been rejected, and the Envoy has.returned to to communicate to King Milan the Bulgarian reply, . THREATENED ADVANCE OF TURKEY. AGITATION IN BULGARIA. :- SOFIA.. WEDNESDAY, 4.30 P.M.— The Servian Envoy Charged by King Milan to treat with Prince Alexander con- "riling the conditions of the armistice has proposed the , evacuation by both belligerents of the positions occupied ,•,,, by their armies on each other's territory. . Some. TuzsuAy.—Lebib Effendi and Gadban Effendi, the Turkish delegates, have arrived at Harmanli on their . Way to Philippoplis. The whole province is in a state of , agitation, and it is feared that disturbances may occur ' should any attempt be made to exercise pressure from with- Out. CONSTANTINOPLE, TUESDAY.—Consular reports received . here state that a great agitation prevails at Peilippopolie in . regard to the approaching arrival of Lebib Effendi and • Gadben Effendi. Turkish military action is believed to be ' Imminent. It is stated the Turks not only intend to enter Roumelia, but also contemplate permanently occupying , the Balkans. It is stated that if Turkish troops enter ' Roumelia they will not wear the fez, but the Bulgarian . kalpack. The Porte contests the right of Prince Alexander to negotiate peace independently. It is, however, pointed ' out in diplomatic circles here that the Khedive negotiated directly with tha Soudan sheikhs without the intervention of the Sultan. Daring the last few days rumours have been Current that Austria and Germany had withdrawn from the Conference on the grouhd that the unanimity necersary tor Ite resolutions could not be obtained. Although the sudden Ilenvocation of the Conference to-day has .given contradic- -1 mon to these reports, it is expected that the sitting *ill be 'rery short. Said Pasha' sole reason for summoning the Conference is understood to be to announce the military , ectien to be taken by the Porte. , , IMPENDING INTERVENTION OF TURKEY. . , PRILIPPOPOLIS, Turruesney.—Lebih Effendi and Gadban , e Efteadi, the Turkish delegates have *arrived here, A meet- `ug was held last evening at the residence of the BishOn. ~, Which was attended by most of the citizens and a few re- presentatives of the provinces. The proceedings were opened , suY the Bishop with a short speech. He said in conclusion, .. 'We can listen to no proposal for a restoration of tho status wi, %ante: no matter through what sources they rney come." lea m men of the province have requested the dele- gates to return at once to Constantinople. Great excite- ment has been caused throughout Eeastern Roumelia by the probability of Turkish intervention. The action of the Porte will, It is stated, have the sanction of Russia, Austria, , and Germany; but the Roumeliots protest that in no cir- cumstances will they consent to the restoration of the : 3tatus quo ante. , THE BURMESE WAR. '. UNCONDITIONAL SUBMISSION OF KING TFIEEBAW. : The following telegram has been received at the Ad- miralty from Rear-Admiral Sir F. W. Iticaards, K.C.8., r Commander-in-Cbief in the East Indies, dated at Thavet- tne Yo, 30th November:—" 271 h, Woodward reports 28th i of truce met flotilla close to nva,viishing to make terms Peace, and begging for armistice. General's reply was I . ' Surrender of King, his army, and Mandalay flotilla.' : Anchored of Acta, 8 eau., 27th, when envoy returned with :. order, from King to accede to all demands. Army sur- rendered forts' 28 guns, and laid down its arms. General Proceeds to Mandalay to-morrow.',' The following has been received at the India Office from ' the Chief Commisioner, dated Rangoon' November 30th, 155 :--4, On the 261 h It royal barge, with a flag of truce, , ruet the flotilla 30 miles below Mandalay, with a letter beg- ging for an armistice. Prendergast replied demanding the . atirrender of the King's army and Mandalay. Next morn- ing the convoy reT tuned with orders from the King to ace Cede to all demands. The army surrendered Ave forts, twenty.eight guns, and laid down their arms. Prendergast : ultended to proceed to Mandalay on the 28th." RANGOON, MONDAY.—The British expedition was met at Iva on the morning of the 27th by envoys from King 1 heehaw, who offered unconditional surrender of all points to the British. As soon as the disarmament of the Burmese , troops is campl,•ted, the expedition will proceed to Man- dalay The war is virtually over. RANGOON, WEDNESDAY.—King Thebave has surrendered unconditionally to the British, who have occupied Mandalay Without fighting: BRITISH FORCE IN MANDALAY. The following was issued on Tuesday from the India ' Office i.....“ From the Viceroy, let Deeembir. The Govern- merit of India is very sensible of the expressions of ap- proval which your lordship has cpnveyed to it on behalf of i her Majesty and her Government. General Prendergast . deserves the utmost credit for the gkill, humanity, and decisive promptitude with which he has conducted the ; whole business. It is a matter of great importance that the °hiects of the expedition should have been obtained without engendering any hostile feeling between ourselves and the - People of Upper Burtnah, who are akin to our Burmese i Subjects in race, religion, and material interests. I propose , to convey to General Prendergast, and to the officers and ; troop, who have so nobly seconded their commander's elects, the thanks of the Indian Government. I have in- structed our agents in Upper Burmah to administer the -- country preivisionally in her Majesty's name " ...MANDALAY. SIINDAY.—The British forces have entered ~ saandalay. Tilers was no resistance. All the European y residents were found to be safe. Ave ONDAY (VIA MIN.) —On the arrival of the . ~ tatina' Mnff kyouttoun, eight miles from Ave, on the 28th, IT of King Theebaw's steamers was seen approaching, steamer, with another, was hastening to Mandalay, b - ying left Myingyan three days previously, when it Was Stopped by three of the King's Mini,ters c,,ming hastily the river in a native bolt, and bearing a letter to Ilerwral Prendergast proposing an armistice. Obsery big British steamers approaching in force, the vessel, which itertaed Seven guns and was we', barricaded, anchored near , 'ita .. shore and hoisted a ittg ef truce. Immodiatelv I,2reearde 300 Burmese soldiers deserted, leaving artillerymen and ri&men behind them. The , s'untateta rowed to Circeral Prendergast's steamer

and presented the letter, which purported to come from the King, but did not bear either his seal or signature. The British commander immediately cespatched them with the letter to the King, calling upon his Majesty to surren- der himself, his country, and his army, and requesting A re- ply by four o'clock the following morning, failing which the bombardment of his town would continue. The Bur- mese steamer wag subsequently manned by the British. Her value is £lO,OOO. The Burmese prisoners state that the King was unwilling to wage war, but the Queen and his relations urged that course upon him. No reply from the King having been received by four*a.m. on the morning of the 27th, General Prendergast ordered the flotilla to ad- vance. When nearing tiagaing the King's boat was sighted approaching at full speed. It brought a reply fromlbe King declaring that he acceded to all the British demands. His army here, numbering some thousands, are rapidly piling their arms. The British landed and took possession of all guns, rifles, ammunition, tied equipm.mt.. Had the King's envoy arrived five minutes later the bom- bardment would have been commenced, the ships, with the Naval Brigade and artillery, hung drawn up in position, and orders having been issued to bombard. The natives express themselves delighted at laying down their arms, and complain very much of the bad treatment they have received from the King and his Ministry. Women and ) children took refuge behind temples and entrenchments, be- ing greatly afraid of the English shells. The equedren proceeds in line to-morrow to Mandalay. where Thebaw and his household are expected to surrender. Flags of truce are everywhere displayed. The King bad a large army here well supplied with guns and rifles. Earthworks were well constructed, and artillery skilfully placed in position in the fort. Had more time been given to the enemy it is thought that aiptabborn resistance would have been met with, but the rapid movements of the expedition surprised the Bur- mese.

THE CAROLINE ISLANDS. Roma, TUESDAY.--ACCOrding to despatches received at the Vatican yesterday, the new Spanish Cabinet has ac- cepted the Pope's decision regarding the Caroline Islands question. THE SOUDAN.—REBEL ADVANCE. ' CAIRO, MONDAY.—A large body of Arabs being seen near Geniss, south of Aka,sheth, the Mounted Infantry the Hussars, and the Egyptian Camel Corps advanced in skir- mishing order. Many shots were fired, and some of the enemy were killed. The Lotus steamer, supporting the movrtm!nt, frequently fired on the Arabs. A man of the Egyptian Camel Corps was wounded, and two of the Mountsct Infantry are missing. They are supposed to have been killed. The main body of the enemy is fronting Kos- hay, south of Akasheh. Consielerable numbers are reported north of Akasheh, thus intercepting the land communication. Large numbers of Arabs are extending from Dongola along the .banks of the river as far as Akasbeh. Spies report that another body, numbering 2,000 men, has eight field pieces and many cimels carrying ammunition. The numbers of the Arabs are s.id to be increasing, and their attitude is menacing. SKIRMISH WITH ARABS AT SU AKIM. SuAatm, WSDNESDAY.—WhiIe A party ef mounted infan- try of the Shropshire Regiment were out patrolling this morning, they were attacked by a force of two hundred rebels mounted. on camels. One private was killed, and a sergeant had a narrow escape. The rebels had two killed.

FRANCE AND TONQUIN. Pants, Mow AY.—ln the examination to-day before the Tonquin Commission, General Briere de L'lsle said that when ha left Tonquin in October there were no Black Flags... It is a police, not a military, force that is needed to make the Delta a happy land. The Chinese hailed the treaty of peace with joy. PARIS, WEDNESDAy.—The Minister for War has received the following despatch from General de Courcy, dated No. vember SO I have intercepted a telegram in plain lan- guage addressed to M. Citable, editor of the•Tonquin offi- cial journal, stating that the majority in the Committee of the Chamber appointed to examine Tonquin credits are in favour of the evacuation. This despatch, were it generally known, would cause great ferment in Annan and Tonquin, both antonz the literates and mandarins." General Campenon has sent the following reply : "The Government and Ministry for War will strenuously defend the.occupation, and complete conquest demanded by De ' Conroy." SPAIN.—FUNERAL (IF THE KING.—PROVINCES IN A STATE OF SIEGE. MADRID, Smetay Noox.—Tha funeral of King Alfonso took place this morning. The responses having been solemnly chanted in the Royal Chapel, the funeral proces- sion started. The streets were thronged by many thousand spectators, and the route to the Northern Railway Station was lined with troops. The hearse was covered with magni- ficent wreathes of flowers, and as the funeral corteye passed the people respectfully raised their hats. The Royal train 'left for the Escurial about mid-day, the body being accom- panied thither by Senor Alonso Martinez, Minister of Grace and Justice and Chamberlain, and other high officials of the Palace. MADRID, SATIITMAY EYENINCI.—A seats of siege has been declared in the Basiine provinces and in Andaluisia. A state of siege has been declared in Old Castile. A revolu- tionary agent is reported to have arrived in the northern provinces, with important papers.

Sevuximv.—Tie Temps publishes a telegram from Venice deseribing an interview between its corres- pondent and Don Carlos, in which the latter is represented to have expressed his conviction that the Regency would be unable to preserve order in Spain for any length of time. Don Carlos reserved to himself the right of intervening in Spanish affairs at the proper moment in order to restore order, and added that he would not legislate to have re- course to civil war should such a step prove necessary to secure the country's welcome. 'GERMANY AND JESUIT MISSIONS.

BErtme, SA.TURDAY.—In the German Parliament to-day Dr.Reichensperger. of the Centre party, brought forward an interpellation regarding the proceedings of missionaries in territnrios under German protection. Prince Bismarck, re- plying to Dr. Windthorst's remarks, declared that the recall of the Jesuits was impossible. It was untrue that only evangelical missionaries were admitted to territories pro- tected by Germany. The fact was that only Jesuit missions could never be allowed. German Catholic missions could, however, be admitted, since it was to be presumed that they would be animated by national sentim( nt. TPIE CIVIL WAR IN PERU.—SEVERE FIGHTING

IN LIMA. NEW Yonx, TIMRSDAY.—A telegram received here from Lima, of yesterday's date, announces that severe fighting occurred in the centre of the town on Tuesday night. An armistice was agreed upon yesterday morning, to last until mid-day. The number of killed and wounded in Tuesday's night's fighting is believed to 19e inconsiderable. Much damage was done to property. Subsequent despatches state that the conflicting parties have arcived at a settlement, and have signed an agree- ment, according to which a commission is to be termed to elect a provisional President. who shall ordera general elec- tion to be held.

Upwards of £l,OOO have been claimed. ' "

DROWNED IN A DrsusED WELL.—An inquest was held on Tuesday, at Sralybridee, on the body of Mary Ann Stott. an old woman, who WAS drowned in a disused well on,Satnrday. The owners of the property knew nothing of the existence of the well, which was abandoned a quarter of a century ago. THE QUEEN held a grand Investiture of Knighthood at Windsor Castle, on Wednesday afternoon, when a number or Orders of St. Michael and St. George, and of Knights Commanders and Companions of the Bath were conferred. The Queen will leave Windsor Castle about the 18th instant for Osborne, where Her Majesty will spend Christ- ' MIS- TEE ',VAR OFFICE has issued a return of the total num- ber or cases of sickness, death, and admission to hospital in the Nile expeditionary force from March 12th up to the present time, and in the Souakim Field during the present year. In the former force there were 4,945 cases of sick- ivs.' and 320 deaths ; in the latter 4,649 cases of sickness and 226 deaths. ' THE Bism CASE.--In the case of Maskelyne v. Bishop, in which damages to the amount of £lOOOO had been awarded against the well-known thought-reader for a libel, which amount had been subsequently reduced to £5OO, an Application was en Wednesday mane to the Queen's Bench Division for a new trial on the ground that the damages were still exceseive. The application was dismissed, with costs. SusprecTEP Munnge.—John Wright, a wood turner, liv- ing at 44, Eloesom-street. Oldham-road, is in custody charged with having caused his wife's death by violence. The parties had, it appears, been living very unhappily to- gether. On Wednesday morning, after cries of " murder! bad bee b heard, the house was entered by some of the neighbours, and Mrs Wright was found lying dead, her hus- band standing beside her. The account he gave was that she bad tallen over a chair. He was on Wednesday brought before Mr. Headlam at the City Police Court and re- manded.
