div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 5. 1885
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 5. 1885

THE ELECTION CAMPAIGN. Tun MAYOR OF GRANTHAM having voted in the Parlia- mentary election, the Conservatives of the borough are about to institute legal proceedings against him. OBJECTION AGAINST R. PARNELL'S HETTIRE.—A Cork telegram states that an objection has been lodged against the return of Mr. Parnell, on the ground that he was wrongly described oil the voting paper as leader of the Irish people. Mn. HEALY'S .ANTICIPATIONS.—After the declaration of the poll for North Monaghan, on Monday, Mr. Healy, the elected member, said in the elections which were taking place in England they found the Liberal and Tory parties evenly balanced, and in the next Parliament Mr. Parnell would wield a pretty big stick over the heads of both these parties. SIR C. Dmitn.—Sir C. Duke, speaking on Saturday even- ing at a meeting of the Liberal electors of the Ealing Divi- sion of Middlesex, said he aid not believe if the Conserva- tive party got into office that they would be able to continue in office upon an alliance with the National party. An alliance between the National party of Ireland and the Tory party could not be held together without concessions being made which would wreck the future of the Conser- vatives. bin. CHILDERS AND HIS DEFEAT.--Mr. H. C. E. Childers has issued a farewell addreas to the electors of Pontefract. He recalls his long connection with the borough, and the promises he received at the last election, ad states that, though warned beforehand of the course of the election, he declined, out of loyalty to his old constituents, all the in- vitations he received to contest ether constituencies. In conclusion, he says, "My attachment to you has therefore cut short toy public career, but that career has ended honourably." INTIMIDATION.—" I hear (says a London correspondent) that information is pouring in from the Liberal agents in , all parts of the country that they have proofs of the eaten- I sive practice in intimidation during the election. The Liberal agents state that in Northamptonshire it VMS gross and flagrant ; and I believe, also, that in the Basingstoke Division of Hants it was extensively carried on. There is no doubt that there will be many inquiries before the elec- tion judges, and in all probability a good many returns will be declared void." ME. FORSTER AND BRADFORD.—The return of W. E. Forster for central Bradford by a majority of over 1,500 has, it is stated, caused much surprise and annoyance to the Irieh leaders, who, on the faith of apparently reliable local reperts, have publicly expressed their belief that the Con- servative candidate would be elected by a majority of at leest 200. The local party managers have reason to believe that the virulence of the Irish attack upon Mr. Forster had the effect of inducing several hundred Moderates, both Liberal and Conservative, to cast their votes for

him. MR. PARNELL AND HIS AMERICAN SUBSCRIBERS.—Mr. Parnell, en Monday, received the following telegram from New York:—" Art enthusiastic meeting of representative American citizens was held to-night in the Roffman Howie, New York, in aid of the Parliamentary fund. Eight thousand dollars were immediately received, and measures taken assuring the collection of 100,000 dollars within the next thirty days.—Euusten KELLY, chairman of the Executive." "The 60th Regiment tenders you a review oil your visit to New York. Answer if you accept.—JAS. CAVANAGH, Colon I." MR. PARNELL'S ELECTION FOR CORS.—Commentiog upon Mr. Parnell's election for Cork, the Dublin Express says :—The whole constituents number 15,000, and of these no fewer than 7,320 remained away from the polling booths. Is not that fact more significant than the 011 for Mr. Parnell ? Does anyone imagine that if they approved of the Parnellite programme they would not have responded gladly to the appeals addressed to them with persistence and vehemence to vote for the League and its leader. We venture to say that their silence and reserve were an emphatic protest against the agita- tion and its leader. It is without precedent that one half of a great constituency should remain away from the polling booths at a critic ii time. if their opinions accord with the policy which they are rallied upon to support by

their votes. SIR H. CROSS ON THE ELECTIONS.—Sir E. Cross spoke at Aorefair, near Ruabon, on Saturday. He said the great battle of the electors had begun in earnest, and tke boroughs of England had spoken out with no uncertain sound. (Cheers.) Their verdict was that they would not have those men to. reign over them aaain who had so misruled the country for the last five years. Birmingham, with its Caucus no doubt, remained where it was; but go IO the great cities of Liverpool and Manchester, and the great towns of Sheffield, Preston, Bolton, and Blackburn, and they one and all told the same story. It was not only the boroughs in England which had spoken thus, but a Welsh constituency, the Denbigh Boroughs, had set an example to the Principality which he believed would be followed
el9ewhere.

EXCITEMENT IN DuBLIN.—On Tuesday evening, on the declaration of the return of the four Nationalist candidates for Dublin, there was tremendous enthusiasm. Mr. Sullivan and Mr. Harrington addresst-d the populace, describing the contest as a vexatious one and a questionable line of policy for the Tories to adopt. The speaker exhorted the multi- tude to behave peaceably. Precessions paraded the streets with placards recording the victory, and American flags. The air rang with cheers, and the refrain of .• God save Ireland." The gates of Trinity College were closed early, and the students not permitted to go out. Large bodies of police were stationed in College Green, and marched along the outskirts of the procession. A band of youths placed an American flag round the shoulders of the Grattan Statue, and fastened it with green ribbon, but the Trinity College students sallied forth and carred it off.
I ment

MR. HERBERT GLADSTONE.—Speaking at the National Liberal Club, London, on Saturday evening, Mr. H. Glad- stone, M.P.' remarked, amidst general cheering, that nothing was so likely to change the attitude of those in the Liberal party who were favourably disposed towards the Church as to witness the supporters of that institution throwing them- selves into the arms of the Tory party. With regard to the future, be thought the proper course for the Liberal party to pursue was—whatever the results of the rest of the elec- tions—to allow the Conservatives to remain in office. Nothing would :tend se much to show the fallacious arguments which heti been put forth by the Tories as to allow them to , have the opportunity of trying to carry them out if they dared. He felt confident that as soon as ever the Tories tried to deal with the Irish question they would find them- selves in a hopeless dilemma, and that it would eventually have to be settled by the Liberals. This question would have to be satisfactorily disposed of before any other ques- tion in which the people of England were interested could be proceeded with, and be predicted that Mr. Parnell would find he bed made a mistake in tbe attitude, he had adopted towards the Liberal party. TRH MEETING OF PAELIADIENT.—TIIII SPEAEERSHIP. —The announcement that the new Parliament will not meet for the despatch of business until February is in ac- cordance with common expectation. In the proclamation of the 18th inst. dissolving the Parliaeient of 1880 the writs of summons are made returnable on the 12th January, and it is in accordance with °worn that Parliament should meet on that day. The proceedings in January will now, it is understood, be limited to the election of a Speaker fled the constitution of the House by the swearing in of mem- bers. The Speech from the Throne will be delivered in February. There will arige in January two questiens—the election of Speaker and the appeal of Mr. Bradlaugh to the new Parliament. Lord Salisbury has, it is understood, given no positive intimation, but it is not expeeed there ; will be disagreement as to the reappointment of Mr. Peel as 'Speaker. It is said that it would be an anti-Conservative policy to adopt any other course. This feeling, which is very general, will go a long way. It is thought that if the Tories had a majority, and were to propose Sir Matthew Ridley for a Speaker, the office might never again rise above a partisan character. and many Conservatives are op- posed to setting an example which they think could not fail to lessen the authority of the Speaker. MR. T. P. O'CONNOR ON TRIP. IRISH VOTE —Mr T P O'Connor save :—Of the 30 seats which the Irish vote attacked in Lancashire they have won 25 and lost.five. The gains are—Blackburn 2, Preston 2, Stalybridge 1, Warring- ton 1, Asbton.ancier-Lyne 1, Birkenhead 1, Bolton 2, Liver- pool 9, Oldham 1, Salford 1, Stockport 2, St. Helena 1, Wigan. The losses are—Barrow 1. Bury I, Oldham 1, Sal- ford 1. All the seats in London won by the Conservatives are wholly or partly dui to Irish votes. The three seats, in Leeds ware a great and unexpected Irish vic.ory, the Irish having counted on only returning two. The three Conser- vative victories in Sheffield were all due to the Irish vote. Mr. Childers was turned out by the Irish vote in Ponte- fract,there being about 180 Irish voters there. A strong appeal was made to except Mr. Childers from the manifesto, but he could not be spared, and the Irifeh voted against him. Similar appeals were made on behalf ot Mr. Slew- Lefevre• but he was decided against, and he is well beaten.— Mr. T. P. O'Connor states that the Irish victories of Satur- day's polling were North Islington, Tynemonth, Peckham, Walworth, Newington, and the Egremont Division of Cum- berland, The Irish electors in the last-mentioned constitu- ency, it is stated, numbered 1.200. The return of Mr. Cowen at the head of the poll for Newcastle-on-Tyne is also re- garded as an Irish victory, the Irish voters having been ad- vised to plump for Mr. Cowen. Ma. GLADSTONE OTHE ACTION OF THE PARNELLITIIS.— Mr. Gladstone on Monday sent a letter in reply to a long address to him from a number of Irish citizens of St. Louis, U.S., drawn up by them immediately after the resignation of the late Liberal Government In the course of the address the signatories say :—"Speaking as representative Irish- men we use no flattery in stating that you are the first Eng- lish etatemman since Lord Fitzwilliarn who has attempted to mitigate the miseries of the Irish people, and we feel grate- ful to you for it. We cannot feel otherwise than grateful,

and ws wish your return to power with increased strength ' and greater power to perfect the reforms you have propoeed for Ireland." Mr. Gladetone'a reply is. as follows: ' " Hawarden Castle, Chester, November 30.--Gentlernen, . The opportune publication of your letter in the St Louis Republican reminds me that it has not yet received from mt the fall acknowledgment which it so well des,rved. I Mr very grateful to you for your words of genuine kindness, and, moreover, I am convinced that they speak the general sentiment of America. I have them before me at a moment when the Liberal party, which alone has ever made strenuous effort to redress the grievances of Ireland. Ic described by Mr. Parnell as the party which consigns her citizens to chains, imprisonment, and death. As having been tbe leader of that party for the chief part of the last 20 years, I am well aware how large a share of the weight of this accusation, if it be a just one, must rest upoa me. Whether just or not it has been the signal fer a systematic co-operation of Irish Nationalists and English Tories in the

present elections which has taken from us and won for Toryism between twenty and thirty seats. 1 pass no judg- ment upon these remarkable occurrences, and my only reply to the vituperation of the hour is this. Of the more arduone labours of my long public life a large part have been de- voted to the service of Ireland, and the most potent of the motives which have led me at an advanced age to forego a long-coveted repose has been and is the hope of possibly be- ing allowed to render her some further service.—With re- newed thanks, I remain, gentlemen, your most faithful sera vant, W. E. GLeztterotex.—To the Gentlemen signing the letter in the Republican of tbe 11th November, 1885." , Mu. GLADSTONE ON THE IRISH VOTE.—Mr. Gladstone on Monday, addressed a meeting at Buckley, Flintshire, The right hon. gentleman spoke of the dual Liberal candi- datures in several places, ad said that but for the tom- foolery of throwing away in this manner four Metropolitan seats, the borough members would have consisted of 112 Liberals arkd 111 Conservatives, instead of 108 Liberals and 115 Coneervativee. The delusion of Fair 'Trade had also misled many urban electors, but the main cause of the Liberal reverses in the boroughs was the Irish vote. What we wanted in this country was the voice of Ireland from Ireland, the voice of England, Scotland, and Wales from lEngland, Scotland, and Wales. That was not the voice twhich some of the counties of Englaod bad been returning. Lancashire bad returned a voice, but if we listened to her accents we should find they were tinged strongly with the Irish brogue. (Laughter and cheers.) Mr. T. P. O'Connor had thrown a flood of light upon this subject in a letter addressed to the Freeman's Journal, in which he sets forth in detail the effect of the Irish vote upon Lancashire, Yorkshire, and other elections' and he thinks he shows, and he was not far wrong, that 25 seats had been carried over by the Irish vote from the Liberal to the Tory party. (" Shame.") Take those 25 seats that we have lost through the Irish vote; add those 25 seats to the 112 which would have been ours but for the present which we have made in London to the Tories; 25 and 112 make 137. Take those 25 seats from 111 and leave 86, and the true numbers , therefore, had the matter been fought without this infusion ' Of the Irish vote, would have been 86 for the Tories and 112 plus 25, or 137, for the Liberals. (Cheers.) That showed that the nation, is a Liberal nation. (Loud cheers.) He believed the Irish were by nature a Liberal nation, but the Irish had been forbidden to vote upon the grounds of general politics, and had been told that their one duly was simply to weaken the Liberal party without any reference to this political question or that. (" Shame.") But, notwithstand- ing, and judging according to the elections up to Friday night, he thoraght the Liberals had seen the worst. If Scotland and Wales continued the good work they had al- ready so well begun, and if the counties showed gratitude to those who had extended the franchise, the Liberals might gain such a majority as would enable them to meet with an independent and imperial spirit any demands which Mr. Parnell might make. ELECTION DTSTURB A/ICES. At Bromley, on Monday, two men were sentenced—one to 14 days' and another to one month's imprisonment—for brutally assaulting the police during an election riot at Chiselhurst. The police were severely beaten with stones and bricks. A sergeant's ribs were broken, and a constable's thumb bitten through. On Sunday night, in Dublin, a disorderly Nationalist mob, while proceeding down York-street, stopped before the Conservative Working-men's Club, and clamoured loudly to have the "Union Jack," which is displayed in the front of the house, hauled down. This being refused, a rush was made to gain an entrance to the premises, but this was pre- vented by the memleers promptly closing the door. The mob then vented their anger by smashing the windows, and did not desist in their mischief till a body of police arrived and dispersed them. Several free fights occurred, resulting in about a dozen persons having to go to the hospital. Two policemen were badly hurt with stones. On Monday night election disturbances took place at Barnsley, being for the most part brought about by youths, 12 or 14 years of age, who first began to throw a quantity of stale fish about. This was followed by stone throwing. Large glass windows at the Duke of York Hotel were smashed, as were also windows at the Trafalgar Hotel and various business places. The mischief was of the most wanton character, the premises of Liberal and Conservative tradesmen being alike attacked. The return of Mr. Pryer- Jones. the Conservative candi- date, over Mr. Hanbury Tracy, for the Montgomery Dis- trict has resulted in considerable diaorder. Smashing of windows and street fights began on Saturday at Newtown, when the banner of the Salvetion Army was torn to pieces, and when the rector of Newtown was also attacked and his coat taken from him and thrown into the river. On Monday, the platform from which Mr. Pryce Jones intended is deliver an address was throwe into the Severn, and several panes of glass in his warehonee were broken. A batch of prisoners were taken before the Nottingham magistrates on Saturday charged with rioting and damage. In some cases fines were inflicted, and in others the pri- soners were remanded, Centinued complaints were made of the conduct of the police on the night of the election, many substantial persons, including aldermen, having been treated in a disgraceful manner. On the other hand, the police suffered severely, and it was reported that one of the Derby constables, who was frightfully injured by a stone, bad died. Heavy claims for damages will be brought against the authorities The polling for Tunbridge Division (Kent) took place on Monday. A large crowd Resembled outside the Rose and Crown Hotel. Tunbridge, the Conservative headquarters, cheering and hooting alternately. About five o'clock in the afternoon the crowd became 110 uproarious that it was deemed necessary to barricade the doors and windows of the hotel. Rotten eggs were thrown in all directions, and almost every pane of glass in the front of the hotel was smashed. Free fights ensued. A large body of police were called out, and until a late hoar !n the night the greatest excitament pre- vailed in the town. FACTION FIONTS IRELAND.—During the contest on Wednesday between Mr. Callan and Mr. Nolan for the North Division of county Louth, extraordinary scenes of violence took place at the village of Carlingford. A mob armed with bludgeons, and stated to be headed by priests, took possession of the town and prevented hundreds of Mr. Calico's supporters from voting. Many persons were injuied.

THE NEWTON ELECTION : RETURN OF SIR IL A. CROSS. On Monday the electors of the Newton Division of South-West Lancashire returned Sir Richard Assheton Cross, the Home Secretary in the pre- sent Administration, as their representative in tke newly-elected House of Commons. For seven- teen years past Sir Richard Cross has represented South-West Lancashire, but this extensive and po- pulous division was by the operations of the Redis- tribution of Seats Bill, passed by the last Parlia- ment, divided into seven portions, and of these Sir Richard Cross, in reply to a memorial, consented to become a candidate• for the representation of the Newton Division in the Conservative interest. This announcement was not long succeeded before it be- came known that the newly-formed Liberal Council of 300 members, representative of every part of the division, had unanimously chosen Col. George McCorquodale, J.P., of the Willows, Newton, as their champion for the suffrages of the electors. In bringing forward a candidate to oppose the return of so well-known a Cabinet Minister as Sir Richard Cross, the local leaders of the Liberal party well knew the tremendous task before them, but, un- daunted by the apparently hopeless character of ousting a Cabinet Minister, they determined that it should not be said of them that through fear they allowed a representative of the opposite party to ' have a free seat. This determination aroused a com- mendable spirit of enthusiasm among the rank and file of their followers—the struggle was entered upon with an earnestness of purpose and a persever ring and increasing hope of success, that when the polling day drew near, it became obvious to the Liberals that, but for the defection of the Irish voters, victory would crown their efforts. For the past few weeks the candidates and their suppor- ters have been hard at work throughout the Division im- pressing their claims upon the electors. Tnese efforts have been folly reported each week, and will be fresh within the recollection of our readers. Suffice to say that the canvas- sers of each party gave in rePorti to their respective " head- quarters" as to the successful nature of their labours. Each claimed to have secured promises of support from the majority of the electors, and confidence as to the result of the election was manifested in many ways. At first the Conservatives seemed to consider the defeat of Sir Richard Cross an utter impossibility, and almost scouted as rash, if not madness, any serious opposition to his return. But the persistent labours of the friends of the Liberal candidate, coupled with his own personal worth and high estimation in the hearts of those who had known him best and longest gradually shook their confidence. and as to whom would first achieve the honour of attaching "M.P." to his name. So far as the claims of the two candidates are concerned Col. McCorquodale, by his unstinting generosity to all classes, his kindness to everyone, and his thorou thly honest and etraightforward character seemed far and away above his political opponent. But his past kindly and charitably in- clined disposition has been forgotten by some of those who have the greatest cause to thank him ; what be ha e done for them in the past has been of little moment during the past week or two, and this unchristian spirit has been displayed by those from whom better things might have been ex- pected. The candidates were nominated at the Newton Town Hall , on Tuesday week, when the returning officer (Mr. S. Brig- house, of Ortnskirk) received three nominations in favour of Sir R. A. Cross, and seven on behalf of his Liberal op- ponent. Each candidate addressed meetings of his sup- porters each eveaing during the remainder of the week. while on Saturday Colonel.McCorquodale spoke at meetings at Earlestown. Ashton. and Golborne. A remarkable enthu- siasm was manifested at these gatherings, and the week closed with public opinion about equally divided as to what -could be the verdict of the electors on the following Mon- day. A large amount of electioneering literature was circulated and distributed among the voters. Pamphlets and plac ads 'III almost every conceivable political subject were printed for the enlightenment of those whose privilege it was to re- cord votes. Reasons why they should support the respective candidates were issued without end,the Catholics and Irishmen were appealed to by the Liberals to remember from what party they had received their privileges and rights, while

the Conservatives, stiugAt., their assistance by publishing Mr. " inanilesto,r dec. The " Fair Trade" theories were coutrovertial ilud exposed, whiLi. questions affecting the colliers and farinars were also brought proini- neatly before their notice. • THE POLLING. led dull, but -'" irds bec.•

The day of polling opent. dull, but afterwarue oecee. brighter. With the exceptien of the Viaduct Waggon Works, belonging to the London and North Western Rail- way Company, the workshops in the district were closed, and several of the places of business were alio eloped. At the Waggon Works, however, a large number of the workmen failed to turn up at breakfast time, and so im- probable was it that the men would return at nbon that the works were closed at one o'clock in the afternoon. In every other respect the day was observed as a general holiday. The Newton Division is one of the most extensive in area I of the Lancashire divisions, and its estimated population of 52,000 is representative ,of almost every section of the working classes. There are numerous coltieries employing a large number of workmen, particularly in the Haydock and Ashton districts; cotton mills at Golborne; railway works at Earlestown ; and the division likewise includes a large number of the recently enfranchised agricultural labourers. The number of voters on the register is 9,344, and they are situated in the various districts ree follows: Ashton-in-Makerfield, 1,523; Hillinge Chapel End, Billinge Higher End, and Winstanly, 601 ; Golkorne, 744; Haydock, 875; Newton (including &Hee own), 1,980; Reinford, 536; Rainhill, 352; Rixton-with-Glazebrook, 159; St. Helens (leccleston, Parr, Sutton. and Windle), 986; Great &whey (Bold, Cuerdley, and Penketh), 511 ; Warrington (Poulton-with-Fearnhead and Woolston-with-Martinscroft), 558; Winwick (Burtonwood, Houghton, Southcroft, Croft, and Winwick), 519. The principal polling station was at the District Infants' School, Market-street, Earlestown, where the Newton and Earlestown electors voted. When the pelting commenced one of tbe first to record his vote was Colonel Geo. McCor- quodale, the Liberal candidate, who was received with ap- plause. The committee rooms of the Liberal party were situated at the corner of Grant-street, opposite the school. The work was carried out under the management of Mr. I Charles Pilkingtern, J.P., Mr. A. C. McCoiquodale,J.P., Mr. ' James McComb (Liverpool), and other gentlemen. The Conservative party had secured the adjoining shop as a committee room. Each building WO covered with election placards, and flags and banners were suspended from the windows. As the day wore on the numbers of persons gathered about the streets largely increased, and as the numberless private cerriages conveying votere to the polling station passed to and fro they were greeted with cheers mingled with hisses. Many people—females as well as men —wore party colours, red and white beinglthe distineuish- I ing marks of the Liberals and blue of the Conservetives. The two candidates drove about the Division during the day and were received with cheers from thAr respective sup- porters. Colonel McCorquodale and Mr. Fergus Kennedy, of Liverpool, afterwards walked to the centre of the Market Ground, where they addressed a few words of encourage- meat to the electors. Some time afterwards the I Conservative party, headed by Mr. Marcus Brown ; Westlvad, Mr. Barron, kc., went to the same spo. ' and attempted to hold a counter demonstration I 1 The attempt was, however, a failure. As evening advanced , the excitement at Earlestown increased, and the crowd swelled to many thousands. Party feeling ran high, and on several occasions it was extremely difficult to prevent a I serious rupture of the peace. Blows were struck in more than one instance, hut there was no general disturbance. Between seven and eight o'clock 50 or 60 juveniles paraded the streets, waving the colours of the Liberal party and singing popular songs. They were not interfered with, though the procession must have been provoking to the more excitable of the Conservatives. The next large rol- ling place was at the Locel Board Offices, Ashton. Tee voters numbered 1,523 and during the day the polling lees I steady. Golborne is en extensive mining district, and it was felt ; that the majority of the 774 voterahere had apprecia- ted Colonel McCorquodale's reply to their question., and would vote Liberal. The polling place wee St. Thomas's ; Church Schools. A similar district in character was Hay- dock, having 875, and the Colliery Schools were utilised as a polling station.—ln Billinge, notwithetanding the decision of the Wigan Farmers' Club, the farmers in this district are supposed to have gene in a body for Sir Richard Cross, Whilst Colonel McCorquodale pined tee chief support of I the miners. The St. Helens district comprises Reinford, with 550 eleetors, and the four townships of Ecctestore Parr, Sutton', and Windle, which constitute the berough of St. Helens, with 986 electors. There were two polling booths in the National Schools, Reinford, entl two in the Cowley British Schools, College-street, St. Helens. Colonel McCorquodale WAS assisted in the district by a number of earnest Liberals, and amongst the gentlemen who lent carriages and other vehicles were Lieutenant-Colonel W. W. Pilkington, J.P., Lieutenant-Colonel Richard Pilkington, J.P., Colonel Gamble, J.P., Mr. H. S. Hall, J.P., Mr. J. C. Gamble, J.P., Alderman Johnson, Mr. W. Gamble, Mr. D. Gamble, Mr. R. G. Brook, and Mr. Thomas Roberts: Mr. J. P. Mearns, as sub-e:ection agent for Colonel McCorquodale, was very energetic in the discharge of his duties. GREAT SANKEY. The presiding officer in booth No. I was Mr. Percy Daeies, solicitor, Warrington, the poll clerk Mr. R. C. Minton, and the personation agents Messrs. Thomas Welsby and Henry Hughes, of Penketh. In No. 2 booth Mr. Henry S. Thret. fall, solicitor, Southport, was the presiding officer, the poll clerk Mr. Alfred W. Dashper, solicitor, Southport, and the personation aeents Messrs. Peter Naylor and Walters. The townships included in this division were Great Sarkev, Cuerdley, Bold, and Penketh. There was little excitement, and it was estimated that the majority polled before twelve o'clock. There were many illiterate voters, and the usual declarations had to be made. WIN WICK.

At Winwick, St. Oswald's School was the polling station, and Mr. Charles Jackson Holmes the presiding officer. The number of electors is 518. Mr. Richard Clark officiated as poll clerk, the personation agents being Messrs. Win. Wright and Louis Bircball. WARRINGTON. The voters of Poulton, Warrington (ownership), Wools- ton, and Martinscroft, polled at the Infant School in Cairo- street, Warrington. The neighbourhood of the booth was rather busy. hut there was no unusual excitement. The presiding officers were Messrs. J. V. Watson, solicitor, Southport, and A. A. Botham, solicitor, Stockport. The poll clerks were Messrs. J. Strong and J. Horsley, of South- port. The psrsonation agents for the Liberals were Mesbrs. S. Dunbobbin and Blair, and for the Conservatives Messrs. R. Johnsen and T. IL Cross. DECLARATION OF THE POLL. The whole of the boxes:did not arrive at the Town Hill, Newton-le-Willows' where the votes were counted, until after eleven o'clock. Mr. S. Brighouse was the returning officer. The crowd outside the hall swelled to large pro- portions, hut there was no disorderly behaviour. Shortly after 12-30 Mr. S. Brighouse declared the result of the poll to be--

div.head: Sir Richard Cross 4414 Col. Geo McCorquodale 4,031
div.p: Sir Richard Cross 4414 Col. Geo McCorquodale 4,031

Majority The announcement gave rise to cheers, which were al- most drowned in a storm of groans, hisses, and whistling. Sir R. Croes,n hen the result, was first declared in the Town Hall in presence of the candidates and officials, proposed a vote of thanks to the presiding officer for the manner in which he had conducted the business. Colonel McCorquo- dale seconded the proposition, complimenting Mr. Brig- house on the impartiality he had shown in cmdecting his Important duties. In acknowledging the compliment, Mr. Brighouse said his only regret was that he could not declare both candidates elected. (Laughter.) The result was then declared to the crowd from the Town Hall windows. Col. McCorquodale has been congratulated on all hands on the gallant fight he has made' and universal regret has been ex- pressed that he had failed to secure the seat. He has, how- ever, given the position of Sir R. Cross a severe shaking, and is in no wise cast down by the result. The polling was excessively heavy, for out of a total reg- ister ef 9,344, no fewer than 3,506 votes were recorded. The following table shows the number polled in each part of the division : Place.

Number on Total register. polled. Ashton 1,823 Colborne Elnine 6,11 Haydock - 815 Newton (Including Earlestown) ... 1,980 }Worm d Italnhlll llixton-with-Glazebrook 159 Eit Helens and Zeelestan 986 Pankey 51l Warrington and out-districts 858 Winwiek, Croft, and Burtonwoxi... big ... -...-- —.—

Totals 8,344 The Liberals claim to have polled a majority in Rain- hill, Golborne, Ashton, Eirleitown, and hiaydock. The Conservative majority Is said to have been made up in Rix- ton, Sankey, Winwick, St. Helens, and Warrington. In the last two places the constituency consists chiefly of free- holders. The Catholic vote in Newton and Itarlestown was split up, the priest in the district being a strong Conserva- tive. It is also stated that a solid body of 200 Irishmen in Earlestown followed the advice of Mr. Parnell, and sup - twirled the Conservative candidate. This item alone was sufficient to decide the election. •

div.head: NEWTON DIVISION.
div.p: NEWTON DIVISION.

LIBERAL MEETING AT EARLESTOWN. A crowded and enthusiastic meeting of the sup- porters of Colonel George McCorquodale was held in the Viaduct. Institute, Earlestown, on Saturday afternoon. The audience spent a few minutes in singing the Liberal songs "March, boys, march," "Auld Lang Syne," &c. The chair was occupied by Mr. Charles Pilkington, J.P. (Haydock), who was supported by Colonel McCorquodale, Mrs. and Miss McCorquodale, Mr. Henry Broadhurst, M.P., for the Bordesley Division, of Birmingham, Messrs. Fergus Kennedy (Liverpool), G. Segar (Liverpool), T. Worthington (Wigan), A. C. McCorquodale, J.P., N. McCorquodale, W. Urquhart, G. W. Rawlins, D. Williams, P. Hall B. Harrison, J. Prescot, W. Gilmour, B. Corlett, J. Evans, P. Thomp- son, Joseph Lythgoe, J. Ormand, J. Gooding, Rev. F. N. Shimmm, and others.

!' Mr. A. C. Mr..ConcrnonALE announced that a letter bael been rec-ived from Mr. Ghuistone expressing a wish for the success of 'Colonel McCorquodale„ and telegrams expressing , th-ir imihility to attend the meeting had been received from ' ,Sir William Vernon Harcourt, 'Mr. Herbert Gladstone, Mr. Holt (Liverpool), Mr. T. R Potter, Mr. W. 14. Forster, Mr. Hibbert, anu others. He said those communications showed they had the Grand Old Man and other leaders on their Side. (Applause.)

The CEAtiname, who was warmly received, said their can: didate came tiefore them for the last time before the election, and be had great pleasure in seeing so many people there that day to hear Colonel McCorquodale's address. (Ap- plause.) Referring to a placard which had been issued by " twenty large employers of labour," he said Se wished to I r give a word of warning about it. The placard stated that many things had been said to induce them to vote for Col. McCorquodale and against Sir Richard Cross, some without any foundation some calculated to deceive, and many alto- gether false, and they (the signators of the circular) en- deavoured to put before them a true statement of facts. (Laughter.) Mr. McCorquodale came before them that day - earictly as he came to there at first; he had never changed front and he stuck to what he bad said in his address like a , man. (Applause.) Of those twenty names only nine were employers of lahour, and though the circular stated tbat if the prekent condition of affairs continued, the only alterna- tive would be emigration or starvation, yet four out of the nine were doing goad business, so that they had only fire who could with any truth speak of the alternative suggested. (Applause.) That being so, what reliance could they place in the circular ? ("Notre.") In conclusion, he asked them to give the free votes of a free people on behalf of the party who had given them their political freedom. (Cheers.) Colonel McConQuoneae received an enthusiastic wel- come. He briefly commented on the circular issued by the " large employers of labour," and said if he had made any misstatement in the whole of the contest he would be pre- pared to withdraw it; but there was not a man in the whole division of the county who valued the truth more than he did, and he challenged his adversaries to show him one mis- statement he had made during the whole contest. (Ap- plause.) He next alluded to tire question of Foir Trade, and said thatin Sir Richard Cross they had a man who sup- ported such Protectionists as Mr. licroyd, Mr. Chaplin, and Mr. James Lowther; and they must judge a man by the company he kept. (Applause.) He said he (Colonel Mc- Corquodale) was the first in that division to urge the sub- stitution of School Attendance Committees for Boards of Guardians for the payment of school fees; and in regard to the Tithe Question he was in favour of all absurdities and improprieties being done away with. (Applause.) In con- clusion, he believed that the questions put to him had been answered to the setisfactson of those who put them and of all who heard them. (Applause.) It was his duty to thank them all who bad attended at the meetings they had held. And.more particularly, It was his duty to thank their chairman, Mr. Charles Pilking,ron, for the great kindness he had shown in the election; and he also thanked the mem- bers of the committees for the attention and assiduity they had shown in their work. (Applause.) If they were suc- cessful ne would have great Cause to thank them ; he had had a great deal of ple,rstee in the contest, which had brought him into more intimate acquaintance with the working-men of Lancashire. It was for them to consider what they would do on Monday; would they vote for the party which did all in its power to deprive them of the franchise, or would they support Mr. Gladstone, the Grand Old Man? (Apolause.) lie hoped and believed they f would vote" jmnock." (Cheers.)

Mr. T. WORTHINGTON (Wigan) next addressed the meet- ing. He remarked that that was the night before the bat- tle, and he hoped they would all rise on Monday morning full oi life and vigour determined that no man should re- main unpolled, and no Man remain unadvised to vote for Col. McCortmodale. (Cheers.) Mr. H. BROADHURST, M.P., who Was then called upon, was greeted with prolonged cheers. He expressed great pleasure at being able to attend that meeting in support of their old friend Col. McCorquoclale. (Applause.) They had heard a good deal from Sir R. Cross with regard to the extimsion of the franchise, which he claimed had been given to the peaple by the Conservatives (" Oh "). He remem- bered attending a meeting some years back in that district when a deMonstration was held, attended by thousands, in favour of extenling the franchise to the counties and bringing about a thorough distribution of political power, which were refused by that incarnation of Toryism, the House of Lords. Those were facts which no one but a Tory would deny. (Laughter and applause.) He thought that if they had at that time dropped the franchise and gone bn with the House of Lords agitation it would have removed a cancer which would relieve the body politic for all fu- ture time. He asked the electors of Newton whether they, who had been said by Sir Richard Cross ta form a degraded electorate, were now going to lick the chains with which the Tories had sought to bind them. ("Never.") The Tories had only given Way on account of want of courage and not from any sense of justice, or right or confidence in the people who were going to have a vote. (Applause.) The speaker next referred to the circular which had been sent out that day, and alluded to his awn election, when he opposed a large employer of labour, and said he had no doubt the men of Lancashire would maintain their name for independence and courage on Monday, and would not let that attempt of their employers influence them, but would rather regard it as a still greater spur to lead them to secure a victory for Liberalism in that election. (App'ause.) He referred to the claims put forward by Sir Richard Cross for a Tory success in the settlemement of the Russian and Egyptian questions, and said a more absurd, fraudulent claim was never set up than those claims set up by Sir Richard Cross to the sac ceases in Russian diplomacy and Egyptian finance. (Ap- plause.) The speaker then referred to the manifesto of Mr. Parnell, and said that if the Irish people who resided in that division were willing, in obedience to one man, to vote against the party which had secured for them civil and religious liberty, that was their business ; but history would cry shame and degradation—(applause)—upon a people who could so far forget their independence, their courage, and their past life. Is conclusion, he asked the voters to support Colenel McCorquodate, for they could not have a more fitting man to represent that division in Parliament. (Applause.)

Mr. GEORGE SEOAR (Liverpool), spoke ori the subject of free education, and said he believed they would get more from the Liberal party than from the Conservatives, and he appealed to his co.religionists, the Catholics, not to be mis- led by the Tories in that matter. He therefore urged them to support Colonel McCorquodale. (Cheers.) Mr. KENNEDY proposed :—" That this meeting congrat 'stets the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone on the splendid ma- jority with which be has been returned to Parliament by the electors of Midlothian, and pledges itself to assist to the best of its ability to return Colonel McCorquodale for the Newton Division of Lancashire," (Applause.) Mr. P. HALL seconded the resolution, which was unani- mously adopted, and a vote of thanks to the chairman con- chided the proceedings. ASHTON AND GOLBORNE.

Colonel McCorquodale afterwards drove to Ashton, where he addressed another large meeting of his supporters. In the evening of the some day, the Gol borne Liberals held a crowded and enthusiastic meeting in the British School- room: The meeting was characterised hy the greatest unanimity throughout. Mr. John Unsworth. presided, sup- ported (in addition to the candidate) by Mr. Norman McCor- quodale, Mr. G. Seger (Liverpool), Mr. F. Kennedy (Liver- pool), Mr. Provaud (Manchester), and many local gentle- men.—The Chairiman said that meeting spoke highly of the Liberals of Golbarne. As a Roman Catholic, he hopecrall his co-religionists would vote for Colonel McCorqmodale. —Mr. Fergus Kennedy, in a vigorous speech, said this was the first time they had an opportunity of retdrning a Gov- ernment of the people. With the triumphant return of Mr. Gladstone—(loud cheers)—he believed the Tories had " shot their bolt," and that it would be seen that the , Liberals would triumph in the counties and throughout the remainder of the country. (Lend applause ) Mr. Provand, in an interesting speech, reviewed the bene- ficial measures paced by the Liberals daring the last forty years.—Colonel McCorquodale, is addressing the meeting, said he started the contest with the determination not to say anything that was not true, and he honed and believed be had carried it out. (Cheers.) The Tory party had said false statements had been made, but he denied that in foto. (Renewed cheers.) If returned to Parliament nothing I would give him (Colonel McCorquodale) greater pleasure than to assist the Grand Old Man in his efforts to reform the land laws, and to offer tbe right band of fellowship to their krethren in Ireland. (Loud applause.)—Mr. Hawkins proposed "That this meeting begs to congratulate the Right Hon. W..E. Gladstone on his brilliant victory in Midlcthian. and pledges itself to use every legitimate endeavour to secure the triumphant return of Colonel McCorquodale at the election on Monday next."—The motion was seconded by Mr. Openshaw, and supported by Mr. George Sego. who was heartily cheered. He said as a Roman Catholic he felt it would be a great mistake for Catholics to stand aloof from their principles simply because they did not agree with the educational views of certain men of the Liberal party. (Cheers.) He urged Catholics net to trust the stick-in-the-mud Tories—(laughter)—but to loyally sup- port their principles, and return Colonel McCorquodale at the head of the poll. (Loud applause.)—The motion was carried without a dissentient voice.—The usual votes of t hank a were passed, and the meeting terminated with hearty cheers for Colonel McCorquodele, and the singing of the strain, "For he's a jolly good fellow." SIR RICHARD CROSS AT NEWTON. A large meeting of the supporters of Sir Richard Cross was held on Saturday in the Town Hall, Newton. The Public were admitted by ticket. Captain Seton presided.— Sir Richard Cross said many months ago he was asked what he thought of the general election, and he was told that when the Franchise Bill passed the Constitutional party would be swept away from the earth. He had great faith in the people of the country that they would rally round their party and return the great Constitutional party to power. (Applause.) One of the great objects that they bad at heart was to maintain for every individual in this country the greatest possible amount of individual free- dom. What had been the verdict of the country so far ? Tbe people had endorsed every sentiment he had put before them, and would go in and win. (Loud cheer!.)—Mr. W. F. Gooch moved a resolution pledging the meeting to return Sir R. Cross to Parliament —Mr. Morrison, of Liverpool, seconded, Mr. Carson and Mr. R. Pierpoint, of Warrington, supported, and it was carried.—Au overflow meeting was held in the old drill-ball, presided over by Mr. John Pear- son, of GolbOrne Park, and addressed by Sir Richard Cross, eMr. M. B. Westbead, and Mr. Carson.

THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, DECEMBER .5, 1886*

SIR RICHARD CROSS has succeeded ill getting returned for the Newton Divisioe_; but he has been saved from defeat—to use Scriptural phrase—by "the skin of his teetb.,, With an electoral roll of 9,344 voters, hi' majority is 383 only, or, to put it in another way, if 192 of the Liberal electors who have, on this occasion voted Tory had vote°t straight, Colonel MCCORQUODALE and ofe Sir RICHARD CROSS would have been it member for the Newton Division of SOO: West Lancashire. The Home Secretary seeot in the first instance to have thought his Pos'd tion impregnable. Had he not fought conquered Mr. GLADSTONE himself in Soatu,:t West Lancashire, and was it to be thoug"e that a man new to Parliamentary wale would have any chance against him? „b could afford to treat such an antagonist indifference, and so he did for a time, until,l,ft gradually began to dawn on the mind of RICHARD that the new electors might ,lafter all, be very enthusiastic about voting a member who had done all he could to Pret; 'vent them getting votes. He then bega° bestir himself; but all his efforts would been of no avail if Mr. PARNELL had ,rl- - to his rescue with instructions to losild; men to vote Tory. There are some hundre of Irishmen in the Newton Division Wlitcl; under ordinary circumstances, would v°ilg Liberal ; and the transference of the blip of the votes of these electors to Sir RICOASaiI CROSS more than accounts for the sts majority that the Home Secretary secured. Besides this exceptional conditr,ii , of things, a difficulty has arisen with Eag`lif ICatholics who have become unnecessorlnf alarmed on the Education Question. ; MCCORQUODALE, from the very first- before Sir RICHARD CRoss entered uporl t campaign—was emphatic in declaring he was not favourable to Free Educat,llo- - that he was desirous of removing al`;r4 equalities that existed between JPiq'tit Schools and Denominational Schools. this went for nothing with unscrupulous ,"`of ponents who were busy sowing the seeosna dissension between Liberal Catholics '3lt4 ;Liberal Protestants. Next to Newton, C‘,/ 1.980 voters, ,comes Ashton, with I,s"cf: Lord GERARD, who is the principal laArl owner in this district, is a Catholic all" 3 Tory, and there can be no question that.na number of Liberal Catholics in the Divisl-to have been misled by false statements as„,,ss ‘• Godless education " and Gool`rs. schools." Taking these two adverse fac,t°4. into account, it will be seen that, if the .09, tie had been fought on pure party Col. MCCORQUODALE would have been rits turned by a considerable majority. it is, he has had a very large peruell-„lo of the votes of the new electors "wo have, all through the campaign, and a great amount of enthusiasm. oice, worked hard for the man of their cAh-tbst The Tories do not seem to have realise-r an, those who were about to exercise the 'I. art chise for the first time were for the rpoSt against them, and they made themsei.ra ridiculous up to the last by talking or majority of 1,500 for Sir .m.ICHARD C 0 be Colonel McCoRQtronALE has proved to the very best candidate that tne Likersi could have brought forward. " If he does nu' meet all the claims of the Radicals, he does b not alienate moderate men, and he holds Y the GLADSTONE programme in its entirety; He has been defeated under circumstance whioh can scarcely arise again; he comes out_ of the contest with honour if not with colour! flying; and if he can be induced to fight another battle we have confidence in saying that he will be victorious.

THE result of the election in the Widnes Division is another striking instance of the influence of the Irish vote in Lancashire. Widnes has, politically speaking, gone to the,. bad by returning a Tory with a wajolity 1,677. When Mr. E. K. MUSPRATT was,. selected as the Liberal candidate, it was fel; ,he was a strong candidate in a strong Liberal

Division. The Tories recognised this, and, for a long time, they were fruitless in their endeavours to find a champion of their cause. In bringing Mr. EDWARDS-Moss for- ward, it was thought that he had little chance of winning ; and so he had, until it became apparent that the Irish electors—of whom there is a large number in Widnes—were dis- posed to act on the advice of Mr. PARNELL and go over, bodily, to the enemy. The polling of Wednesday shows that they have done as they were told—they have voted Tory and given the Tory Candidate a large major- ity. It is particularly hard on Mr. MUSPRATT that he should have been treated in this way, for his past career shows that he has ever been a stout friend of the Irish race, and, further, that he has always been opposed to a policy of coercion. But the word had gone forth against him; it has been obeyed; and the Tories are, for the moment, made happy. There are not a few Conservatives who evince .great anxiety to discount the Irish vote; they do not like their new allies; they think Tory- Parnellite "sounds bad ;" and they would soon cut the connection, if they could do it with safety to themselves. As they cannot do that, they delude whom they can by talking of a Conservative reaction. But the facts are against them; there is no mistaking the factor that- has been in operation, when it is seen that the great successes of the Tories have been in Lancashire where the Irish vote is large, and that the reverses ot Lancashire Liberals have been in proportion to the strength of the Irish vote. Mr. T. P. O'Cox- NOR, who has been the "head centre " of operations, claimed, at the beginning of the week, that the Irish had wrested zs seats, in Lancashire alone, from the Liberal party; and Mr. GLADSTONE, referring to the matter at Buckley, on Monday; accepted the statement as correct. It went, of course, in the direc- tion of giving emphasis to his demand for a majority against tbe Tories and Parnellites combined, in order that the, members of the House of Commons may legislate as free men. The great leader of the Liberal party cannot but feel saddened to think that he is being ill repaid for his vast and beneficient labours on behalf of the Irish race; but he has not lost heart, nor has he lost the magnanimity of disposition which reveals "a kindness ever nobler than revenge." Dis- coursing on the situation to the electors of Flintshire, he said : I have not a word to say against our Irish fellow- citizens. A great deal of my life has been sent in the humble endeavour to do justice to them. (Cheers.) And, gentlemen, recollect, however the Liberal party may have suffered at this moment, and however the interests of the country, through the Liberal party, may have isiffered through their error and mistake, recollect, when you revolve the pages of former history, that much allowance is to be made for them, and, whatever irritation their present conduct may produce, never let it cause us for one moment to slacken in the desire to give them everything that justice can claim, and seal, if you can, the good works that have marked recent years by what can - Ite those works. (Loud cheers.)

Should they, however, insist upon holding what they call "the big stick" over the .heads of the English, they will find that they have made a mistake; five millions of people are no match for thirty millions

MR. BRUNNER has won a splendid victory in the Northwich Division; 1,028 is a magnifi- cent majority fora section of Tory Cheshire. It is the outcome, of course, of the extension of the franchise.; and it is thus that the old order giveth place to the new. Runcorn has shown itself loyal and fervent in its Liberal- ism, notwithstanding the disreputable at- tempts that were made by the Tories to in- fluence votes by suggesting that the growth of Winnington meant the decay of Runcorn. The inhabitants of the incient port have sense to see that they can hold their own in a fair field ; and that if they should suffer in any particular the VERDINS are not the men to help them out of the difficulty. The Liberal candidate nailed his colours to Lie mast; and he comes out of the contest as he went in—earnest, resolute, and clean-handed. He made no secret of it that he was an advanced Reformer, and he has shown such a knowledge of the abuses he desires to remedy that he has per- force carried his hearers along with him. In addressing the enthusiastic ,crowd after the declaration of the poll, Mr BRUNNER said he was proud of the victory because he had been elected as a Liberal, while there had been a signal failure of the attempt to send a man to Parliament because of his trade. He struck a responsive chord when he asked them to send whearty message of congratula- tion to Mr. LATHAM for the great victory he had won at Crewe. Mr. LA:rwmathas so often .stormed the Cheshire stronghold in vain that • there is something of poetic justice in his .being the first,kto break down the barrier of ' Tory monopoly ; and the rejoicing at his success is general, because in this last fight he has had ,to struggle against intimidation, at Crewe, of the most glaring and shameful kind. With men like. Mr. LATHAM, Mr. BRUNNER, and )MR. BROCKLEHURST, as re- presentatives, Cheshire will have a different voice for the future; it will be one that will be worth hearing.

THE Working-men of St. Helens, to the 'number of about 200, have joined an organ- isation, new to this country, known as "The :Knights of Labour." It would seem to have ori- ginated in America, where there are no less than ,5,000 lodges. The objects of the movement •are to dignify and elevate labour and the labourer, and as a means to this end arbitra- tion is advocated, in,mferenee to strikes, as a ,mode of settling disputes. Itis highly.credi- table tnthe artizan ,class that they should set an .example by favouring arbitration. There are many instances already on 'record where employers have refused ,proposais for arbitra- tion on the part of the employed, and it would therefore appear that as to the ethics of labour the masters are as yet behind the men. " The Knights of Labour" are moving in the right direction, but why should theycall them- selves "Knights ?" Is there not something of vanity in this copying of titles, and will it not tend to bring the organisation into ridicule We have Knights and Dames of the Prim- rose 'Teague, but nobody reads of their' doings without a smile, and such is the power of association that we fear "the Knights of Labour" will be debased rather than exhalted by the title they give themselves. Honest Work, well done, carries with it its own title to respect. There is a grand simplicity about LONGFELLOW'S "Village Blacksmith," Which has charmed the world. ' The poet would have spoiled the poen if he had called his smith a "Knight of Labour." "Something attempted, something done" doubtless earns more than 'a night's repose." Let the worthy workman by all means" blok the whole world in the face." "Sons of
I toil," or "Sons of labour," if you will ; but Knights of Labour I Humph! "Take away I that bauble !"

Pdartley. chief agent for the Examiner, h authorised to receive advertisements and news paragraphs All printing orders sent to him will receive prompt atten- tion. • The Mill Brow Brass Band will give their third annual concert on Wednesday evening in the Public Hall, Run- LECTIJRZ AT WIDNES.-Mr. J. B. Imison on Monday evening gave a lecture on the early history of the Church, In Waterloo-toad school. The vicar presided. .

-- WIDNES CHORAL SOCIETY—Under the auspices of this society a concert will be given in the Drill Hall on Thurs- day next. Particulars in our advertisement columns. BETHESDA MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY, RUNCORN. —On Wednesday evening, the Rev. J. D. Thomas, hon. president, read a paper entitled "Christ and Malaomet in Europa." The subject was not common, and great attention was given the essayist. THEATRICAL LICENCE AT RUNCORN.—At a special Ses- sions on Monday, Messrs W. Bankes, A. Thomas, James Elandley, and G. L. Davies on the Bench, a license to perform stage plays at the National Schools was granted on the application of Mr. W. Wnittaker. LICENSING MATTERS AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Thomas Jones was granted permission to sell at the Commercial Hotel, Bridge-street, John Blun- dell, at the Berle. -lOW Hetet, Church-street, and Edward Page, at the Cornwall and Devonshire Inn, Church-street. SUDDEN DEATH AT WIDNES.—On Wednesday night a young woman named Wright, aged 22, daughter of an en- gine driver employed at Messrs. Gasket', Deacon, and Co.'s works, died suddenly In Moor-lane, in consequence of a fleshy formation in the throat. The deceased had been a cripple for a number of years. SOCIAL Priem AT WIDNES.—Mr. Henry Varley, on Monday evening, delivered an address en the subject of "Social purity" to a good andience of men at Milton Congregational Church. Captain Brunner presided.—'Dn the motion of the Rev. R. G. Hughes, seconded by Mr. T. Robinson, a vote of sympathy with Mr. Stead was passed. AN OLD OFFENDER AT RUNCORN.—Catherine MCCOnn made her 19th appearance at Runcorn Police Court, en Thursday. charged with being drunk and disorderly in Cooper-street, on the previous night, and also with breaking a window worth 12s at the Anchor Hotel, Brunswick-street. —She was sentenced to 21 days' hard labour on each charge. A Rummer FLATMAN DROWNED—Arthur Handley, a flatman who lived in Regent-street, Runcorn, was drowned In the Mersey early on Saturday morning; Hindley whilst taking the flat of which he was captain into Widnes dock, was knocked inte the water by the boom, and as he was wearing a heavy coat and seal boots he sank Imme- diately. THE RUNCORN STABBING CASE i-Yesterday, at Runcorn Police Court, George Wilson, seaman on hoard the schooner Agnes Ellen, was brought up on remand charged with cut- ting and wounding John Wyatt, a fellow seaman, on the 27th ult., under circumstances already reported. Dr. McDougall deposed that the injured man was progressing favourably, but was not yet able to appear in court.—A remand was granted until Monday on the application of Superintendent Leah. LACEY-STREET WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE, WIDNES.— The members of this society gave an entertainment to a large audience on Monday eveninc. An interesting feature of the programme was a prize competion for the best dialogue, and the first prize was awarded to Lily Smith and Alice Swindles, who recited "The Ruined Brother." The second and third prizes were awarded to Polly Swin- dles and Annie Ramsey, who had selected "Aunt Tabby's Secret." Mr. John Houghton presided. A CHILD BURNT TO DEATH —A girl aged four years, named Martha Ann, daughter of Thomas Forster, of Rock Savage, died on Wednesday from the effects of burns. On Tuesday, the deceased was left in the house alone, and in a short time a man named Quinn beard her screaming. On going to the house, he found the child in flames. He ex- tinguished the blaze by wrapping his coat round the girl, but not until he had sustained dreadful injuries* which ended fatally a few hours afterwards —An inquest was held on Thursday, at the house of Mr. Joseph Stokes, Rock Savage, when a verdict of "Accidental death" was re- turned. SEARCHING 'FOlt GAME AT WESTON.—Sohn Swatman, a young man, was brought up at Runcorn Police Court on Monday charged with trespassing upon the land of John Morris at Weston, in search of game on the 24th November, P.C. Dale proved seeing the defendant upon a field carrying a loaded gun. He said he was after a " blue back." Mr. Morris said there were hares, rabbits, and partridge upon his land, and the defendant had been warned net to trees. pass open it.—Superintendent Leah said there had been many complaints about the offence. These persons got a 10s. license to carry a gun, and thought they could shoot anything they liked. A fine of ss. awl costa was imposed. LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD INQUIRY LT WIDNES.— Mr. Bard, an inspector to the Local Government Board, held an inquiry at the offices of the Widnes Local Board on Monday, with reference to an alteration desired in the man- ner of the repayment of the loans of the Board. There were present—Messrs. Gossage, Taylor, Handley, Wright, and Allen (the clerk.)—The Clerk explained that the Board wanted the LocalQrovernment Board to fix an annual in- stalment for the repayment of gas and water debts, and that power should be granted to the Local Bond to use that instalment•yrn by year in paying off the debts, and not as at present keeping six sinking fends for loans -fall- ing due at different periods. If this power were granted to the Local Board,,there would, he arguc i, be a considerable saving 'births amount of interest, because, should the money be invested in Government securities the interest which the Local Board would receive would not be more than 21 or 3 per cent. whereas they could use the money in paying off loans which have interest at 4 and 41 per cent. There ti would, therefore,e a saving of 1 to ti per cent. The Clerk then-submitted a complicated statement on the sub- ject. —The Inspector 'expressed his satisfaction with the way in which thwfignres had been placed before him, and said he would report. The inquiry then terminated. Public Analysts have submitted CADBURy'S 0000 A. to close tests, and the result has always proved its great value as a sus- taining and nourishing beverage. Black, in proposing a motion against raffling at bazaars, said the practice was dishonouring to God. The Rev. Mr. M‘Tavish,,in seconding the motion, said the idea of gambling for the cause of God was enough to make any Christian man thrill from head to foot. An amendment in favour of raffling was proposed, but Dr. Black's motion was carried by seven 'votes to two. Tani (GOVERNMENT AND THE ORANGEMEN.—Mr. W. Johnstone, M.P., speaking at an Orange meeting in Dublin, on Tuesday night, said the Orangemen of the North of Ireland were determined to protect their lives and liberties, and to face the traitors and rebels. He nas. not certain whether Lord Salisbury intended to bring in Mine measure to satisfy Mr. Parnell and dissolve the union, but in the name of half a Orangemen he warned the Govern- ment that that very day the Orange volunteers would be mustered in Munster, and if the bill re- ceived the 'Royal assent it would be regarded as a declaration df civil war in 'Ulster. ILLIgEss ON THE NEW MEMBER FOR CREWE.— Mr. G. W. Latham, the newly-elected member for the Crewe Division, is lying at his residence, Brad- wall Hall, seriously ill. On Thursday, in the Crewe Division, rather alarming reports were circulated concerning his health, but a Crewe correspondent inquiring at Bradwall on Thursday evening was informed that he was getting better. He has been prostrated by overwork, the severe strain telling upon his health, and as soon ad he is sufficiently re- covered he has been ordered by his medical advisers to go away for a complete change. Numerous con- gratulatory telegrams and letters have been received from all parts of the country on the gallant fight 'which Mr. Latham made.

' HOLY TRINITY DAY SCHOOLS, RUNCORN. The annual concert and distribution of prizes in connea- don with these schools took place, in Runcorn Public Hall on Thursday evening. There was a large attendance of parents and friends. ;The Rev. R. Preston incumbent, on- `cupied the chair, and he was supported by Bishop Ryle, and Mr. Edward Derbyshire, of Liverpool. On the plat- form were several hundred children, and during the even- ing they sung a number of part songs and glees in a most admirable manner. Mr. T. W. Annett, the head master, was the coeductor, and he is to be complimented upon the suc- cessful result of his labours. Amongst the items on the programme were "The liquid gem," sung by Miss A. Sefton; "The ploughman and the poses," recited by Master J. Malone; "Daddy," sung by Master A Curzon; and the duet "What are the wild waves saying." by Miss Sefton and Master Curzon. The audience showed their ap- preciation of the talents of the young performers by loud and frequent applause. Mr. Annett, by movements of the hand, simply put the children thiough the tonic-solfa scale in a manner which elicited warm plaudits.—The Chairman explained that the object of the proceedings was to obtain a sum of money to be applied to giving those children who atiEnded school regularly a picnic in tt.e summer. He was proud to say that Holy Trinity Schools continued in a most satisfactory and exemplary condition. (Applause.) They had passed this year 96 per cent, of the scholars. I tApplause.) In Runcorn they had had Board schools to I Contend against, and as they knew the new Beard schools in Oreenway-road would shortly be opened. What the char- acter of the teaching would be they could not prophesy, but he could with perfect safety prophesy that it would not be able to beat that at the Tiinity and at the Parish Church schools. (Applause.)—Previous to distributing the prizes, the Right Rev. the Bishop of Liverpool delivered a short address. After referring to his Cheshire origin, his Lord- ship spoke of the value of education. There was no getting on now-a-days without education. Ignorance would no longer do. Without education there was no proares, and those boys and girls who went forth into the world unedu- cated must go to the rear, and have very little chance of improving their position. If education, however, must be of real value, it must be a religious education founded on the Bible, not the history and geograpy of the Bible merely explained, but its principles pressed home upon the hearts and consciences of the children. After offering words of encouragement to the scholars, the Bishop said he wished the Trinity schools every prosperity. (Applause.)—His Lordship then distributed the prizes. RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly m;eiing wag.; held yesterday. Present, the Rev. Canon Barclay (chairman), the Rev. Father Fen- nelley, Messrs. R. Lea, J. Plitchard, and G. S. liazle- burst. THE VACANCY: HR. W. HANDLEY PROPOSED.

. _ . A letter was read from Mr. F. J. Norman thanking the members of the Board for the honour they had conferred upon him in electing him to fill the vacancy caused by the death of his dear father. He expressed his keen regret that his many other reponsibilities forbade him to accept the honour.—Mr. Pritchard thought they would be in accord with the wishes of the ratepayers as expressed at the last election if they appointed Mr. Wm. Handley to the posi- tion. He therefore proposed his appointment.—Father Fennelley seconded—Mr. Haziehurst said his view, and one he had held consistently for eleven years, was that the con- stitution of the Board should be three Churchmen, two Wesleyans, one other Nonconformist, and a Roman Catholic member. They had worked on these lines during the whole period of the Board's existence, and he believed that any deviation from them would be a mistake. The numbers who attend the Wesleyan Chapels outnumbered the Presbyterians and Independ-nts and he did not think they could fairly give the majority and the minority two without running a risk of disturbance on every occasion a fresh Board had to be elected. He understood that Mr. Handley was promised by the party who were properly constituted to give that promise, that he should fill the first vacancy on the Board, and therefore he had nothing further to say, although he could not vote for his appointment. Personally, Mr. Handley was peculiarly qualified for the position.—Father Fennelly said Mr. Handley was to have a seat if Mr. Hazleburst refused to act when appointed. There was nothing said so far as he remembered about succeeding to the first vacancy.—Mr. Pritchard said he was informed that Mr. Handley withdrew , at the last election OA the promise that he should have the first vacancy. He decidedly had the majority of votes so far as the last meeting of ratepayers was concerned—The Chairman said Mr. Handley was only promised the position It Mr. Hazlehurst declined to accept. He did not object to Mr. Handley—quite the reverse, but he did not want him to be elected on a false issue.—Father Fennelley moved that the appointment be postponed.—This was agreed to, and the Board began the consideration of applications for the posi- tions of teachers at the new schools.
