div.p: THIS LATH MR. NORMAL

In reply to the vote of condolence with the family of the late Mr. Thomas Norman, Mr. F. J. Norman wrote as follows :—" Will you kindly inform your Board how thoroughly our family appreciate their condolence and sympathy with us in our sore bereavement. It is the one bright spot in the awfully dark cloud which enshrouds us that our dear father was so loved and honoured by so many kind friends.—Yours faithfully, F. J. NortadaN."

Mr. Gladstone was born at Liverpool on December 29th, 1809. He is the fourth son of the late Sir 1 John Gladstone, Bart., of Fasque, Kincardine, Scot- land, a well-known Liverpool merchant. , He was educated at Eton and Christ Church, Oxford, of which he was nominated a student in 1829 and graduated, taking a double first-class in Michael- mas term, 1831. He was first returned to Parlia- ment at the general election in December, 1832, in the Conservative interest, for Newark. In the House of Commons his mercantile origin, the suc- cess of his university career, his habits of business I and his high character recommended him to the no- tice of Sir Robert Peel, who, in December, 1834, ap- pointed him to a junior Lordship of the Treasury, and in February, 1835, Under-secretary for Colonial affairs. Mr. Gladstone retired from office with his ministerial leader in April and remained in opposi- tion until Sir Robert Peel's return to power in September, 1841, when he was made Vice-president of the Board of Trade and Master of the Mint. The revision of the tariff in 1842 was almost entirely the' result of his energy and industry. When this laborious work was brought before the House of Commons it was found to be as admirably execu- ted in its details as it was complete in its mastery of general principles, and it received the sanction of both Houses with scarcely an alteration. In January, 1846, Sir Robert Peel announced his inten- tion of proposing a modification of the Corn Laws, and Mr. Gladstone, who had Succeeded the late Ear/ of Derby in the post of Secretary of State for the Colonies, adhered to the leader under whom he had entered on ministerial life. Unwilling, how- ever, to remain under obligations to the late Duke of Newcastle, who sympathised strongly with the opposition party, he resigned his seat for Newark and remained for some timeout of Parliament. At the general election, in August,. 1847, he was elected for the University of Oxford, and in the Parliament of 1847-52 he furthered the cause of liberty and reform by the course he took on the questions of Jewish disabilities and Uni- versity reform. He consequently frequently found himself opposed to his former friends; and even- tually separated himself from the great body .of the Conservative party in February, 185/. At the general election in the following July Mr. Gladstone was re-elected for the University of Oxford but only after a severe contest. On ' the formation in 1852 of the Coalition Ministry under the Earl of Aberdeen, Mr. Gladstone was appointed to the I Chancellorship of the Exchequer, in which office his thorough knowledge of finance proved of the greatest ' assistance to the Ministry. Soon after the recon- struction of the Ministry. under Lord Palmerston Mr. Gladstone resigned office, and for some time pre tm independent support to Lord Palmerston's Ministry. In the winter of 1858-9 he accepted under Lord Derby's second Cabinet a special mission to the lonian Islands to arrange certain difficulties which had arisen in the administration of that de- pendency; and in June, 1859, resumed office wider Lord Palmerston as Chancellor of the Ekchequer. In this capacity he was mainly instrumental in re- pealing the paper duty, and in promotins the nego- tiations by Mr. Cobden which resulted in the com- mercial treaty between this country and France. Besides being eminent as a statesman, Mr. Glad- stone had acquired celebrity as an author. His first work, "The State in its Relations with the Church," published in 1838, was followed, in 1841, by his "Church Principles considered in their Results; and these works stamped him, while still a young man, as a deep and original thinker. Mr. Gladstone's "Remarks en Recent Commercial Legislation," pub- lished in 1845, were intended to pave the way for the extensive modification in the restriction, on commerce imposed by the corn laws. During a visit to Naples in 1850 he learned that a large number of the citizens of that place, who had formed the "Op.- ,position" in the Neapolitan Chamber of Deputies, were exiled or imprisoned by King Ferdinand, and that above 20,000 of that monarch's subjects had been thrown into prison on a charge of political disaffection. Mr. Gladstone urged the Earl of Aber- deen to interfere on behalf of these victims of tyranny and that interference proving ineffectual,

he published an indignant letter on the subject of the state prosecutions at Naples, copies of which were forwarded by Lord Palmerston to the various courrs on the continent. In 1858 Mni Gladstone published his elaborate work "Studies on Homer and the Homeric Age." Having been rejected by the University of Oxford at the general election in July, 1865, Mr. Gladstone was returned for South Lancashire, and after the death of Lord Palmerston he became leader of the House of Commons retain- ing at the same time his Chancellorship of the Ex- chequer in Lord Russell's second adminstration. Early in the session of 1886 he brought in a Reform Bill, hut owing to an adverse vote in the House of Commons Mr. Gladstone and his colleagues resigned. In 1868 Mr. Gladstone brought forward and passed through the House of Commons a series of resolu- tions having for their object the disestablishment and disendowment of the' Irish Church. These re- solutions were the basis of the Irish Church Suspen- sory Bill, which, on May 22, was read a second time in the Lower House by 312 votes to 258, but was re- jectedin the House of Lords by a majority of 95. At the general election of the same year Mr. Glad- s Lone was defeated in South-west Lancashire, but, in anticipation of such an event, he had been returned by Greenwich by a large majority. On the resig- nation of Mr. Disraeli's Ministry in December, 1868, Mr. Gladstone became 'Prime Minister, and then fol- lowed what was probably an unexampled series of Reforms. The most prominent of the series were: —The Irish Church Disestablishment Act (1869), the Irish Land Act (1870), the Elementary Educa- tion Act (1870), Abolition of Purchase in the Army (1871), the Ballot Act (1872), and the Judicature Act (1873.) The principal measure proposed by the Government in the session of 1873 was the Univer- sity Education (Ireland) Bill which was opposed by theßoman Catholic members who, voting with the Conservatives, caused the rejection of tne Bill by 287 votes against 284. At the ensuing general election, the returns of which were completed on February 27, 1874, the Conservative members returned num- bered 351, as against 302 Liberals and Home Rulers. On January 13, 1875, three weeks before the assem- bling of Parliament, Mr. Gladstone announced in a letter to Earl Granville his determination to re- tire from the leadership of the Liberal party. The terrible atrocities in Bulgaria, however, brought Mr. Gladstone from his retirement, and he took a memorable part in the agitation respecting those massacres. At the commencement of 1879 he was invited to become the Liberal candidate for Midlo- thian, which invitation he accepted. He set out from Liverpool for Edinburgh on November 24th, and from that date, with the exception of two days' rest at Taymouth Castle, his life till his return to Hawarden on December 9 was a long succession of enthusiastic receptions and unwearied speech- making in condemnation of the policy of the Conservative Government. On the dissolution of Parliament at Easter, 1880, Mr. Gladstone renewed in Midlothian his famous campaign, and by his splendid eloquence carried everything before him. He beat his opponent, the Earl of Dalkeith, sen of the then Duke of Buccleuch, by 1,597 votes against 1,368, and throughout the country 349 Liberal were re- turned, as against 243 Conservatives and 60 Home Milers. After consulting Earl Granville and the Marquis of Hartington, the Queen entrusted the task of forming a new Cabinet to Mr. Gladstone, who himself became First Lord of the Treasury and also Chancellor of the Exchequer. This latter office, however, he resigned in 1883. The principal events of the late Administration of Mr. Gladstone are too recent and well known to need recapitulating, but it may be mentioned that one of these was the ex- tension of the franchise to the county house-holders, which may probably be looked upon as the crown- ing achievement of Mr. Gladstone's illustrious and beneficial career. At the present general election Mr. Gladstone again appealed to the electors of Midlothian, and was triumphantly returned to Par- liament by the almost unequalled majority of 4,631, the figures being : . GLADSTONE (L) 7,879 ' DALRYMPLE (C) 3,248
Majority 4,631

div.head: HEALTH OF THE TOWN.-IMPORTANT REPORT.
div.p: THE HEALTH OF THE TOWN.-IMPORTANT REPORT.

Dr. Macdougall, medical officer of health, reported as follows:—" The number of deaths registered during the past month amounted to 23. Of these 2 were due to violent causes, in which cases inquests were held. Of tbe remain- ing 21 deaths, 5 were due to scarlet fever, 4 to bronchitis, 2 to wasting, 2 to dropsy, 2 to convulsions, 1 to chronic dis- ease of the liver, I to apoplexy, 1 to consumption, I to can- cer, Ito Jaundice, and Ito premature birth. Of the 21 deaths 9 were infants of 1 year and ender, 3 were children over 1 and under 5 years, 2 were over .5 and under 10. Of the adults 2 were over 40 and under 50;. I was over 50 and under GO ; and of the aged 3 were ovei SO and under 70, and 1 was 73. The above 21 deaths show an average death rate for the twelve months of a little over 15 per 1,000 of the estimated population. Scarlet fever is still to be credited with 5 deaths; but there in a gratifying reduction in the number, as well as a diminution in the number of sick cases, as compared with the month of October. I fear that intercommunication continues to •be a fruitful medium of conveying the disease, and unless parents are more careful in isolating their children during sickness, it will be im- possible to check effectually the spread of this scourge. I would like to direct the attention of the Authority to the urgent need of taking greater interest in the supervision of milkhouses. Hitherto nothing has been done in this direc- tion, and it will be manifest to the Board that it must con- tribute very materially to the regular inspection of these houses if,they were to be registered. Milk.eaters so largely into the food of children that when it is offered fer sale it should be pure and wholesome, and of good quality. If milk houses were to be periodically inspected, the Authority would be satisfied that ttey were kept clean and in a satisfactory sani- tary condition; and also that their surroundings were , kept clean and in a satisfactory sanitary condition. An occasional surprise visit would ensure proper attention be- ing given to the repnirements of the Authority in that direction, a matter of no small importanoe in dealing with epidemic diseasee. A correct register of these houses will further enable the Authority to become familiar with the retail dealers' source ofeupplv, and, moreover, will help the Authority to act promptly and with vigour in cases where any of the inmates are suffering from infecting fevers, and where isolation might be absolutely necessary to ensure complete protection te the consumer. The Sanitary Act of 1875 gives ample powers of inspection and seizure to the medical officer of health and to the inspector of nuisances; but with regard to adulteration, generally the police authori- ties have wide powers, and frequently act with energy. I understand that for some time past a person has been in the habit of offering for sale second-hand clothes in the market. I•have made inquiry of the person in question as to the continued source of her supply. She informed me that she always purchased in the Manchester market for her retail trade. It will be apparent to the Authority that this kind of trade may become the mediem of disseminating infections diseases, and conveying to innocent homes the germs of fevers of the most virulent type. During the month a number of structural improvements had been effected, and others are jn course of alteration, and when completed will add very materially to the sanitary state of the pro- perties concerned. The large open asopits, many of which are met with in some parts of the town, deserve the careful consideration of the Authority. An instance of this class of ashpit, which is situated in a close court, was emptied of its contents during the month, a feat which had not been accomplished for many years, and was found to contain 12 cart loads; and from two ashpite in another part of the town no less than 42 cart-loads were removed. On Friday and Saturday of last week I had occasion to make an in- quiry into a very offensive smell that was supposed to have had its origin in the escape of some highly poisonous gases throngh the street grids and from some grids in the base- ment floors of some houses in the north side of the lower portion of High-street. The escape eeemed to rue to be due to sttuctaral defect in the sewer, but it would be well if the Authority would institute a searching inquiry into the whole drainage system of this part of the town. It is im- possible to over-estimate the necessity of ascertaining with some degree of exactness the cause of the escape periodi- cally of those noxious gases, so that a speedy and effectual remedy may be adopted." The report was referred to the Health Committee. WORK IN COMMITTEE.

On the recommendation of the Highway and Sanitary Committee, a sub-committee was formed, consisting of Messrs. Dobson, Speakman, Fisher, Taylor, White, and Farrell, to consider as to the advisability of purchasing a steam roller. it was also recommended that the tenser of Mr. James Kirkham for the erection of a building at the rear of the Town Hall, for the sum of £97, be accepted, such building to be need as a toolhouse and lamp room.— The salary of the inspector of canal boats was increased from £lO to £2O per annum, on the proposal of the Canal Boats Committee.—The Finance Committee reported that receipts for the month amounted to 1..385 188 sd.—Aceounts amounting to £264 13s 10d were passed.—The plans for the barracks of the Salvation Army, in High-street, were passed. There was no other businesi of public interest.

LANCASHIRE CUP TlE.—Haydock e.Romendale, This tie in the third round of the Lancashire Chal- lenge Cup competition was played on Saturday afternoon at Rossendale. The home team on by eight goals to one. THE Holm IRON TRADE.—The English iron mar- ket is on the whole unchanged, and business is still to some extent interfered with by the elections. But there is greater firmness in pig iron, which is, for the time being, unmistakable, and which ap- pears to be based on the general expectation of better trade. The Glasgow warrant market has been steady during the past week, with a firmer tone prevailing than has been the, case for some time. The local trade, however, is still very bad. Scotch pig iron makers, with the 'exception of one or two, find business very dull, and their prices are easier. Closing quotations of warrants, on Wednes- day, were, with sellers, 425. Bd. cash and 426. I.ld. a month; buyers offering one halfpenny per ton less. A good deal of steadiness has been apparent about the northern pig iron trade, and there is less and less inclination to sell pig iron on the part of the makers—iron. RESTORATION OF ST. HELENS CHURCH, HOLLINS- FA.RE.—The above church, which was partially re- stored in 1879, and again in 1882, has now received its final touches by the addition Oa new gallery Of pitch pine to match the nave, a new east window, and other decorations. the new gallery is the work of Messrs. J. and IL Wrighe, Kelsall, near Chester, and reflects the highest credit upon that firm. The east window is the work of Messrs. Thompson, Cross-street, Manchester. It represents the Ascen- sion in the centre, with the figures of st. John and St. Paul on each side. It is the gift of the Cawly family, long resident in the neighbourlictod, and is as, line piece of work. The whole walls and ceilings have been cleaned, painted, and decorate& The chancel has had most attention. The ceiling is struck out in various panels, and richly treated in colour and gold. ,The walls outside the arch of the comsnunion have been diapered and a high dado formed. The walls of the arch have been treated very richly. It contains seven etchings on gold grounds ; the centre one representa the restirrection, and the other forms a furze. The rest of the wail space is filled up with inlay ornamentation and gold.' The work of decoration has been admirably executed by Messrs. T. Hesketh and Sons, art decora- tors, of Warrington. The whole of the work has a very rich appearance, and has been much admired. The floor of the chancel is laid with mosaic pave- ment, and has been carried out under the superin- tendenoe of 'Mr. J. E. 'Wright, architect. The re-opening service took place, on Sunday .week, when there were crowded congregations. _ _

"THE FIVE P'S."—Mr. Chamberlain, speaking at Leicester, on Thursday night, ascribed the defeat of the Liberal party‘in the boroughs to a combination of the five P., viz., priests, publicans, parsons, Par- nellites, and Protectionists, but such a combination was never likely to occur again. He does not think the new Parliament will have a long life. TRIBUTE TO M. MUMMIES. The Financial Reformer or December pays the following deserved tribute to Mr. McMinnies:—" In the retirement from Parliament of our warm and earnest suppor- ters, Mr. Samuel Morley and Mr. McMinnies we have lost two men that couldill be spared just now, but whose rest has been well and nobly earned. For all Financial Reformers like these there lathe glori- ous and undimmed retrospect of having throughout their career aided in cheapening the food, increas- ing the comforts, and lessening the anxieties of millions of their fellow-country.' PROPOSED PUBLIC PARK FOR Si. HELENS.—The Town Council of St. Helens, on Wednesday decided, after some discussion, to adopt a recommendation of the Parliamentary, Improvement, and General Purposes Committee, that they should purchase an estate for the purpose of a public park and recrea- tion ground. For a long time the committee has had under consideration the question of providing such a place for the borough. Negotiations were opened with Lord Gerard, to ascertain the cost of about 130 acres of land lying between Denton's Green-lane; Cowley Hill-lane, and Wincllehurst, and with Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co., for a piece of land near St. Thomas's Cemetery; but while they were proceeding a letter was received from the executors of the late Mr. John Ansdell to the effect that, "Knowing it was the wish of the deceased gentleman that his Cowley estate should beeome the property of the Corporation for the purpose of conversion into a public park, they desired to inti- mate that the property would shortly be sold, and that they were prepared to entertain favourably any offer the Corporation might decide to make." Hence the resolution that, subject to the sanction of the Local Government Board to the borrowing of the mon, y, the Corporation should offer £ll,OOO fo* the purchase of the estate, which, it is understood, consists of about thirty-five acres of ground, a large family mansion, and several cottages. Col. Gamble, J.P., ever ready to assist in the benefit of the inhab- itants of St. Helens, has offered to present to the Corporation, in the event of their acquiring the Cowley Park estate, the triangular piece of land, containg one and a half acres, bounded by North- road, Rutland-street, and the said estate. thereby placing the proposed park within a ring fence of public roads. The committee unanimously accep- the offer. The Town Council on Wednesday cordi- ally thanked Colonel Gamble for his gift.

RETIREMENT OF COLONEL MANSERGR.—CoIOneI o London i i , ' Gazette of the 24th November as relinquishing ManserghS name has appeared in' the the command of the 3rd South Lancashire Regi- ment. The Colonel has since issued a battalion order in which he desires to place on record his ex- treme regret at being parted from his old corps. Of the thirty-two years he has had the honour of be- ing connected with the regiment (he says) he has spent eleven years as its commanding officer. He cannot look upon the period of his command with- out feeling most deeply, the gratitude he owes to the officers, non-commissioned officers and men for ' the cheerful way in which they have always car- ried out his wishes, and for the readiness all ranks have universally shown to support the credit of the corps To say that this has lightened materially his responsibilities in not sufficient; it has also ren- dered his tenure of the command a period upon s which he will always look 'back as the pleasantest of his life. He begs, therefore, to tender his sincere and hearty thanks to all, and in bidding farewell to his comrades of the regiment he hopes that the bright name the corps, has always sustained may. still remain unsullied for all tin*. - SUDDEN DEATH AT VirAEGRAVL—An unusually sud- den death occurred at Wargraye on Tuesday aft-rnoon, when John Jones, 38 years of age, formerly employed as a smith at the Viaduct WriAgon Works, died after only a few day's illness. The thceased remained at work untd Thursday last week, but owing to a feeling of illness he did not return. The attendance of Foulstm, of Eariestown, was obtained, but the suffering man rapidly grew worse, and he expired from inflammation of the lungs and pleurisy on Tuesday afternoon. He leaves a wife and seven children. Tax PROPOSED BATHS FOR Eanmearowar.—The pro- posal to establish public swimming baths at Earlestown has lately taken a more definite shape, and a Committee has been formed with the view of furthering the project. The committee includes the names of alt the local elergy and ministers, and a considerable number of other geutlemen. A circular which has been lamed in reference to the matter states that tbere appeared to be no hope of obtaining any consideration in the price of water to the extent they anticipated, and from inquiries made as to the average attendance in the winter months at various places, includ- ing Tyldesley, Bolton, Bury, Leigh, and Ashton-under-Lyne, such bu,ilding and appliances for heating could not be erected without some guarantee of public support. It was found that not leas than 50 subscribers were required in or- der to meet the expenses of the water supply, which would exceed per week. Inducements were offered to intend- ing subscribers, and it was stated that senior and junior swimming clubs would he formed, the object being to teach and promete the useful art of swimming, and to reward acts of bravery rendered by the members in attempting to or rescuing others from death by drowning. The terms of membership were stated in • full length, and intending mem- bers were asked to register their names with a small deposit as a guarantee of goad faith. It was added that this would give the promoter an idea whether it would be worth while to go on with the building. The circular was forwarded to gentlemen resident in the district, but as yet there has not been a very liberal response. I. will be a regrettable cir- cumstance if the project is allowed to fail through want of support from the public, for whose bentfit it was first mooted.

div.head: AIR. GLADSTONE'S RETURN FROM
div.p: AIR. GLADSTONE'S RETURN FROM
SCOTLAND.

On Saturday, before leaving Edinburgh for Hawarden, Mr. Gladstone addressed two great meetings. At the first be said that Mid-Lothian had surpassed herself in the vote given for hire on lb. previous day as compared with that for Mr. Dalrymple, who throughout the contest had con- ' ducted himself manfully and honourably. He proceeded to vindicate the action of the late Government in regard to the Transvaal, remarking that though they were accused of cowardice and truckling, that was the reward which every man must be prepared to expect who desired to follow jus- tice through evil report as well as good report. The second meeting which be addressed was organized by the working- men of Edinburgh, 4,000 persons being prennt. Mr. Glad- stone referred to the almost unbroken rank of Liberals which Scotland bad returned, and expressed his confidence that Wales would follow Scotland's example. ne attributed the Conservative successes in English boroughs to the Irish vote. HMbelieved that many of the counties would vote Liberal. Mr. W. E. Gladstone left the city at six pm. for Eng- land. After the second meeting be, Mrs., and BEES Glad- stone, accompanied by Lord Rosebery, went to the Cale- donian Station, where the party were loudly cheered by a large assemblage. Mr. Gladstone took tea in a room at the station, and then passed to the train for the south amidst the greatest enthusiasm. The travellers arrived at Carlisle at twenty minutes to nine, and met with a hearty recen- tion. At the station the right hon. gentleman spoke a few words to the crowd on the platform. He said they had never depended upon the English boroughs for the constitu- tion of a Liberal Government. Scotland had done her duty magnificently. As the train steamed out of the station a ting.ing cheer was raised. An immense crowd awaited the 1 arrival of the train at Leckerbie, where the ex-Premier ap- peared at the window of the marriage, and said that he had neither time nor voice to say anything except that Scotland was doing her duty most faitlatully, and, as far as he had beard, the coundes of England were disposed to do thvir duty too. They hail got a most noble example, and he thought they would follow it. (Cheers.) He added that it was rernarkah,e that there were constituencies In the south whlch they had never before been able to reach which were coming over most nobly to the Liberal support. Loud cheers were given for Mrs. Gladstane, who bowed her ac- knOWledgMentM Addressing the company at Preston Station, Mr. Glad- stone said : I understand the Toryism of Pretort to be the Toryism of Fair Trade. Of all kinds of Toryism it is One of the worst. it would b 3 mischityptis if it were possible, but It is totally impossible : and all. those who are now seeking after it will be bitterly disappointed. It is a great discredit to the intelligence of Pr :ston. The Liberals of Preston are

in a minority, and I give them the advice which Lord Beaconsfield once gave," Let them work until they become a majority." About half-past eleven o'clock on Saturday night Mr. Glad- atone arrived at Bank Quay Station,Warrington, on his jour- ney home from Scotland A large number of people, who had assembled on the station platform in the expectation of seeing the right hon. gentleman, gave ringing cheers as the train approached, which wer, again and 3galn renewed. Mr. Gladstone bowed his acknowledgments. Cheers were given both for Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone, as the ttain departed for Chester. Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone arrived at Chester shortly after midnight. Thousands of persons had assembled at the eta- ties, and enthusiastic cheers greeted the train. The con- tiuuous cheering made it impossible for Mr. Glad- stone to speak. The saloon carriage was attached to a special engine and taken to Broughton Hall statien, whence Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone drove to Ha. warden astle. They reached it about one o'clock on Sun- day morning. The right hon. gentleman and Mrs. Gladstone visited the Orphanage before going into the Castle, and sang " Home Sweet Home," the children joining with them. On Sunday Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone, with Mr. Henry Gladstone and Miss M. Gladstone, attemied Divine service in the Parish Church, both morning and -evening. Be did not read the lessons, but seemed in excellent voice and health. Mr. Gladstone has written to his election agent in Mid• lithian expressing his gratitude to the police authorities for their excellent arrangements on the eecasion of the opening of the Mercat Cross, and also conveying his best thanks for the congratulatory letters which have reached I him on his success in Midlothian, especially these from I " the authors of the victory." The right hon. gentleman adds that the note then struck has sounded throughout the I land, and is being echoed back by many a cry of victory.

NEAT DIRECT FROM THE YABM.—The movement among East Kent farmers for supplying meat direct tee the con- sumers, in preference to selling their fat stock in the public markets, is meeting, it is said, with most encouraging suc- cess. Up to the present the advantages of the movement have been enjoyed only by the public in country towns; but in the course of the present week an important con- nection will be opened up with the metropolis, by which means the public in London will be able to buy prime joints at from 2d to 3d per pound less than is now charged. Mrs. Bradley, furniture dealer, Old Hall. street, was going to bed in the dark early on Wednesday morning, when she was attacked by a man who is supposed to have entered the house on the previous evening. 'The fe low cut her throat, and on her servant girl coming to her help she too was attacked in like manner, but was not so seriously injured. As a policeman was mounting tie stairs in responseto the cries of the two women the burglar dropped from the bedroom window into the street and escaped with- out leaving any clue to his identity. The wound on Mrs. Bradley's throat is a very deep one. WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. A meeting of this Council was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening. There were present—the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), presiding, Aldermen Holmes, Kean, and Burgess ; Councillors Dakin, Fleming, W. Pierpoint, Ashton, Wright, Brown, Whittle, lluchinson, Bolton, Green. all, and Francomb ; Messrs. Brook (town clerk). Whittle (deputy town clerk), Longdin (borough surveyor), and Chorley (borough treasurer). WATOR COMMITTBIL This committee recommended as follows :—Resolution, that Mr. Councillor Broadbent be appointed the deputy chairman of this committee for the ensuing year; motet. tie, that the meetings of this committee be held every Thursday; at four o'clock; resolution that Mr. Alderman Kean and Mr. Councillor Jolley be appointed the Visiting Committee of the Bridewell ; resolution, that tne Mayor be authorised to engage sixty constables from the county , of Lancaster, for duly at general election, to be held one Tuesday. the 24th inst.—On the motion of the MAYOR- ' seconded by Alderman 801201455 these minutes were eon firmed.

RINANIH. The Finance Committee recommended the sanction of 'orders for payment of accounts amounting I. £5,0i0 Ss 10d, and accounts in Connection with the gas department amounting to £1,208 2s 2d. It was ales stited that Alder- man Holmes had been appointed chairman, and Councillor Greening deputy-chairman, for the ensiling year; and that Councillor Brown bad kindly consented to audit the col- lectors' accounts.—On the motion of Alderman Hinnies, and seconded by COIIIICBIOr BROWN, the minutes were adopted.

The minutes of this committee were as follows .—Resolu- lion that Councillor Broadbent be appointed chairman. and Councillor Platt deputy-chairman, of the committee for the ensuing year.—Resoiution that the meetings if this com- mittee be held every alternate Thursday at 4-45 p.m., and when summoned by the chairman.—Resolution that the fol- lowing members of the committee be appointed the Lighting Sub-committee: Councillors Platt (convener), Barker, Dixon, Greening, and Wright.—Resolution that the follow- ing members be appointed a Visiting Committee to visit the sites of proposed buildings or alteratioas to buildings when required: Councillors Broadbent, Platt, Greening, Wright, Marsh, and Roberts.—Recommendation that the fallowing plans be approved: Plan of alterations of pattern shops for Messrs. Pearson, Knowles and Co., Limited; plan of pro- posed alterations to offices at Bank Quay for Messrs. Phillips, Putman and Co.—Resolution that the sum of .£3 10s, and £1 is casts, be paid to Mr. Robert Pemberton, and his wall fronting School Brow be re-built, in consideration of his setting back such wall and giving the strip of land to the Corporation.—Recemmendation that the following ' plans be approved: Plan of 14 cottages in New-street, off Battereby-lane, for Mr. John Appleton: plan of stable be- hind premises in Bewsey-street, for Mr. James Skelland, conditionally; plan of bakehouse ia Jackson's Court, for Mrs. Jackson.—Recommendation that the sum of £7OO be paid for six cottages in Lythgoes-lane, belonging to Peter Leigh and others, and that the Town Clerk be instructed to enter into a contract for the purchase tbereof. Councillor Warrant. moved, and Councillor Wkurrma seconded, the adoption of these minutes. Councillor BOLTON asked with reference to the cottages in Lythgoes-lane if it were intended to open Lythgoes-lane down into Orford-lane.

Coencillor WRIGHT said the cottages in question were standing out some 14 or 15 het on the right-hand side going from Orford-lane Clown Lythgoes-lane and the committee thought there would not be a better opportunity of making an improvement than at present, as the trustees were clos- ing the trust. He might tell Otem that some years ago the trustees wanted .£9OO for that property. Alderman BURGISSS suppoited the recommendition of the committee.

WIDNES ELECTION CAMPAIGN- LIBERAL MEETING. Widnes Volunteer Hall was on Tuesday night, the 1 eve of the election day, crowded with an enthusias- tic audience in support of the candidature of Mr. E. K. Muspratt. Every seat was occupied, large slum- bers of people were standing, and there were up- wards of 2,000 persons present. There was an ele- ment of antagonism, which occasionally broke forth in groans, but tile counter cheers given for Mr. Mus- pratt completely silenced the opposition. During the earlier part of the proceedings the speakers had some little difficulty in proceeding in consequence of disturbances at the back part of the building, but Mr. Muspratt and Mr. Segar received a quiet aud in- telligent hearing. Mr: F. IL Gossage, J.P., presided, and amongst those on the platform were Sir Henry. Roscoe, M.P. for South Manchester, the Revs. J. Hathersall, R. Yeatman, and J. Calvert, Captain Brunner, Dr. Cooper, and Dr. Hurter, Messrs. G. Segar (barrister), T. Snape, S. Sadler, F. H. Pank- hurst, J. Tallon, R. Webster, J. Bray, J. Beech, R. 1 Baker, R. Booth, I. Carr, W. Streets, S. Jackson, J. Williamson, S. B. Stringer, J. Jackson, R. Booth, J. Farrant, Joseph Robinson, R. Fogg, M. Taylor, V. C. Driffield, B. Brown, T. Clarkson, R. 11. Davis, E. Carey, F. Gaskell, S. Robinson, J. Morrison, F. Keyes, W. G. Browning, S. Owens, and Thomas Sadler, The CHAIRMAN in a brief speech, said those who thought for themselves, and had the courage of their cenyictions, who believed in the inviolable secrecy of the ballot—(a Voice : "They'll vote for Moss," and groans and cheers)— those men would place Mr. Muspratt at the head of the poll with a large majority. (Cheers.) There was no comparison between the two candidates, for Mr. Moss wee quite unknown, while Mr. Muspratt all his life had laboured hard for the great Liberal cause, for education and for freedom of every kind, and had been associateA with the greatest men of the century—Bright, Cobden and (Had- stone. (Loud cheers.) Sir ilszriti Roscoe, M.P., spoke upon free trade, free land, and free education, in moving That this meeting rejoices in the magnificent majority by which Mr. Glad- atone has been returned to Parliament as member for Mid- kthian, and declares its absolute confidence iii that great statesman's leadership of the Liberal party." (Duette ) Mr. T. SNAPB seconded the resolution, and asked upon what ground were they going to send Mr.. Moss to Parlia- ment ? Mr. Moes would go there to support a party that had always blundered and been guilty of deeds that would not bear investigation if they looked at their pest history. They knew how the Tories premised all sorts of retort-xis, and how reluctant they were to marry those reforms into effect. Their opponents covered themselves with safe- guards to every pledge they made, and when asked to fulfil them they pleaded the impossibility of carrying them out under the difficulties in which they were placed, and the country looked in vela for a fulfilment of these ! promises. (Hear, hear.) One reason why they should have Mr. Muspratt to represent them was because science was progreasing, and education developing, and they wanted men to represent scientifie industries—which 'formed the staple manufactures of Widnes—in Parliament, to speak for them when occasion required. (Hear, bear, and cheers.) Mr. Muspratt was a gentleman of the highest scientific attainments, and they must have—and On the ,following day the polls must show that they meant to have—a representative of the alkali trade. (Cheers.) The resolution was put and carried amid great cheering. Mr. Muspaerr, who received an ovation on rising, dealt with the question of taxation of !Agri, and depression of trade. He wished to make them clearly uedererand that if they had to resort to any of the Tory panaceas of Fair Trade, instead of improving the trade of the country they would do that which would tend to depress the trade of this country more. Sir Henry Roscoe had pointed out to them how in countries like the United States of America and France, who possessed that which the Tories wished the people of this country to poinese—vii, protection to their native industry—that in those countries there was a far greater depression of trade and a far larger number of men out of work than in this country at the present time. (Disturbance.) Did the men he saw before him think that this was not a question for them to consider— whether they would advocate a policy which would give them employment. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) They might depend upon it that the whole principle of Free Trade was to buy in the cheapest and sell in the dearest market, and in order to buy the cheapest and sell the dearest they mast also produce the cheapest. How were they to pro- duce the articles which they did produce cheaper? Amongst the influences which he believed—in fact he was certain—would cheapen the production of tindr manufac- tures he in the first ;lace put the cost of railway carriage. The carriage of goods in this country was on many articles double the rate per mile which it WAS in other countries. Moreover they had foreign produce carried on English railways at a cheaper rate than English produce—(a Voice. "Shame.") These were things which they could deal with themselves, and he proposed, if they returned him to Par- liament, to do all he could to bring about a change in the law, so that the railway companies, who were monopolists, should be forced to reduce their charges upon the carriage of goods. Then there was another question which it was very important they should censiner, and that was the royalties upon their minerals. The minerals were generally owned by these same landlords of whom he had spoken to them, and who had been so careful to look after their own interests on the question of taxation. Tbe royalties upon iron today had been calculated by Mr. L. Bell, a great authority upon iron manufacture, where at somewhere about 3s 61 per ton. The royalty was the earns whether the price of iron was low or high ; and when they talked about the importation of Belgian or German iron into this country—and this had been talked about in the news- papers to a great extent—how did they account for it ? How did Michael Davittaccount for it ? He appealed to the Irishmen present as to whether they agreed with what Michael Davin said upon this subject, and his statement was that the whole difference lay in the royalti,s If they wished to cheapen their manufactures, one of the great means of doing so was to improve the teehnieAl educe- lion of their foremen and artisans. As be h. d indicated on former occasions, there, were industries a hich had found their seat in Germany and not in this country because of the superior education of the German people. We had the raw material in this country, and the first invention in the matter was made by an Englishman, but the manufacture had been carried over to Germany because of the want of the necessary technical education on the part of cur peo- ple. For the very same reason that he had talvm the side ~f the Irish people against the landlords of Ireland, he naked them as Irishmen to help him to: fight the battle they as manufacturers and working-men ot Widnes had with the landowners of this country. (Great cheering, and

Months ago Mr. E. K. Mus- . works. pratt, a gentleman of great scientific attainments, On the motion of Alderman lioranes the minutes were of decided political views, and a local manufacturer confirmed. , was nuanimouely chosen as the candidate by the Liberal . Council, but the'. Constitutional party" could prevail upon . nobody to champion their cause, and it seemed at one tune that Mr. Muspratt was to have a walk over. At length, after name after name had been brought forward, quickly to sink into oblivioo, Mr: Tom Cottingbarn Edwards-Moss, son of Sir Thomas Edwards-Moss, Bart., threw himself i into the breach. His chance against a strong candidate like 1 Mr. Muspratt was considered very shadowy. By and bye, t however, complications were thrown into the contest by the Irish Nationalists. The Irish element in the division is a most important factor. In Widnes upwards of one third of I the population is of that nationality ; the natives of Erin I also enter largely into the composition of Garston ; and the Dien electors in the division add up; to at least 2,000. Under these circumstances it is not too much to say that the Irieb- ! : men are the masters of the situation. Mr. Chamberlain stiropounded his ideas en Free Education, and the Catholic i priests in the locality severely attacked his scheme, and ; charact.erisrd it as an attempt t I tional echoo-. - o eecularise the denomina- te in scarcely veiled language the members ;of their flock were influenced to vote "blue " if this ; were to be a plank in the Liberal platform, and [affairs began to asaunie a threatening aspect for the Liberal candidate. Mr. T. P. .O'Connor paid a • visit to the town, and to an audience of upwards of two I thou:rands of his fsllow-countryrnen assailed the Liberals in I 1 a violent taebion.r After this Mr. Parnell's manifesto Was no surprise. But knowing Br, Muspratt's advocacy of the I claims of Ireland for a long period, Iremembering bow vigorously he had opposed the policy of coercion, end his I popularity amongst the Irish ueople, it was viewed by the English Liberals and the Irish electors with regret that he was nut one of the "exceptions." Hopes, however, pre- vailed to a late period that some movement would be made in his favonr, but these were set at rest. on Saturday last, when the following circular was distributed :—'• Vote for Mr. Tom Cottingharn Edwards-Mose, and obey your leader, Mr.-C. S. Parnell. Do not be deceived by rumours or even petitions, Parnell hae spoken, and he will not unsay what he bite said. The committeeef the Widnes Branch of the Irish National League can say with authority that Sir. Par- nell will not make an exception of Mr. Muspratt. Retnem- her coercion, your leaders expelled from Paaiament, im- prisoned, and even the ladies of your country cast Into a „felon's cell, without the shadow of a charge against their fair name. Remember Buckshot and cruel Forster, by whom your innocent countrymen, Francis Hynes and Myles Joyce, were sent to the gallows, and Bryce Kilmartin even when shown to be innocent, forced to bear the lot of a mur- derer. Now is the day of battle. Strike for your country, and strike hard by voting for the Tory candidate, T. C. Edwards-Moss. Fellow the example 'Of your countrymen in Liverpool, Manchester, Warrington, St. Helens, and other places, and so hasten the day when Ireland will be a nation once again. God save Ireland r Signed on behalf of the branch, Dr. O'Keeffe, president: J. Fitzpatrick, vice- president' G. Faulkner, treasurer; S. Quinn, secretary."' This was followed by a crowded meeting of Irish electors in the Drill Hall, on Monday evening, under the presidency of Dr. O'Keeffe, who announced that he bad pledged him- self to obey Mr. Parnell'. order. A resolution pledging the meeting to support Mr. Moss was also carried without dis- sent. Under these discouraging circumstances, however, the Liberals relaxed not an effort, and on Tuesday evening, i at*a meeting of great proportionse Mr. Muspratt mate a [ stirring appeal to the Irish electors. Mr. Segar, the eminent barrister, who is a Catholic; on the same occasion supported Mr. Mnapratt's candidature in an elcquent speech to his co- religionists, ana it was believed influenced them to some con- siderable extent. But the power of Parnell was paramount. " I'd like Mr. Mtispratt," said more than one native of the Emerald Isle, " to get in, but I must vote for Parnell." And in giving their suffrages to the Conservative candidate , the Irish were voting for Parnell, not Moss. 1 I On tbe morning of the election the walls Were placarded with a telegram trom Mr. Parnell and Mr. T. P. O'Connor to Mr. S. Quinn, bon., secretary to the Widnes National League. It ran," We Lope the Irish electors will stand by the manifesto and vote against the Liberals." Against this could only be placed Mr. Muspratt's clear and satisfactory declarations on Home Rule and religious education, and the prevailing sentiments of the placards issued in his favour were "Justice to Ireland,' "No Coercion," Religious Edu- cation," and "Reform of the Land Laws." "Vote for Mr. Muspratt, your townsman," was also prominently dis- played. The mural literature with regard to Trade, Free Educa- tion, and other subjects was pretty extensive, but Mr. Moss's expenditure upon printer's ink will scarcely be the chief item of his bill. "Vote for Mr. Moss and good trade" was the only placard it was thought necessary to issue, the as- sured help of the Irish vote rendering any extraordinary efforts unnecessary. Bat notwithstanding the predominance of Pernell's influence And the action of the priests, who took an active part in the election, there were Irish and English Catholics who boldly declared their intention to support the party of progress, but their number was. too 'small to affect the result, and they brought themselves into disfavour with their countrymen. The polling commenced at eight o'block on Tuesday morning and progressed with an even steadiness throughout the day. Very few conveyances were employed on either side, most of the electors walked to the booths, and except in the vicinity of the polling stations, a. stranger would not have observed that any event so important as a Parliamen- tary election was proceeding. Most of the manufaccurers gave the workmen an extra hour at noon, and the trades- tnem's establishments were closed aboat three o'clock. Mr. Moss paid a visit to the town early in the forenoon, bot to most of the townspeople he was,a complete stranger, and his appearance in the street created no demonstration. In the afternoon Mr. Muspratt arrived by train. He was ac- companied by his brother, Mr. J.. L. Muspratt, and the gentlemen having seated themselves in an open carriage, a number of ardent admirers unyoked the horses aodoirew the Conveyance bathe Liberal committee-room at West Bank. ; Hearty cheers broke forth at aeveral points on the route, and several hundred spec•ators gathered. Duriog the day Mr. JI T. Brunner, the successful candidate for Nerthwicb Divisien was in the town and 'recorded his owe for Mr. Muspralt. By five o'clock three-fourths of thiselectors had polled. A large staff of policemen had been drafted into the town ready for any emergency that might arise, but the greatest quietude prevailed,, and their servicaa were not re- quired. The town WAS divided, into two polling districts—north and sonth. In the former there were six booths in Simms Cross Board Schools, Ana presiding officere being Messrs. G. H. Danbv, C. EL Lewin, J. A ROYAL BRYFER HALF'S ATTENTION.—A very comical story is going the rounds respecting the Queen of Italy and her husband, whose hair has turned quite white, though he is not more than forty-two. Qseen Marguarite procured from Paris a bottle of highly-recommended hair. dye, and begged her spouse to use it and restore his looks te their original colour. He thanked her, but made no pro- mise. The next morning her favourite poodle came rui- ning up to her; bat, horribile Netts, the creature was is longer white, but bright green! She was very angry, and asked the king what he had been doing. "Merely testing the efficacy of your hair-wash, dear Marguerite, before making use of it," was the reply; "and my next expert- meat will be on your Brazilian parroquet." The queen re- moved the bottle from her husband's dressing-room, and has had ne more to say about his white hair. Matilda Snowball is the coloured Gook of aa Austin family, and is much addicted to Rule society. A few evenings ago she said to Mrs. Peterby, the lady for whom the oondeecencts to cook at fifteen dollars a month : "If yet please, mum, I'se gwine ter pra'r meads die ebenia wid my only brudder, and I'll not be back till it breaks up, so I wants de key ob de front gate." A nice sort of brother he 4, no doubt," retorted Mrs. Peterby, who has her own ideas 1 about coloured prayer meetings. Yes, mum, my !prodder am a gensman. I'se been acquainted win him ober moos I came ter Austin, two yeahs ago." The newly-appointed parson of a very hilly Kentish ! village, being a cricket enthusiast, was resolved to instil a ' lave of the game into his parishioners. Accordingly a ' meeting was held, subscriptions and help were premised, I and the sole difficulty that remained to be overcome was the discovery of a suitable field. The only level bit is the 1 parish belonged to the butcher, who was a cantankerous, iyamptions fellow, lie' however, consented to lend his field: and, although he was known to be so. cricketer, he was ' asked to play in thelopening match. His first ball clean I howled him; bat, instead of walking away from the wicket, he remained, with the evident intention of continuing his ' innings. The umpire therefore walked up to him and said, " You're oat, Mr. Bull, you're out." The butcher tamed rotted and said, "Oh, I'm boat, ham I? I'm hour? Well, horn yea all go from my blooming field!" An American acting manager tells the following story in reference to the late General Grant;—" The first act was over, and we were chatting In the wings with our manager, when one of the boys rushed up to tell us that General Grant arid family were in one of the boxes. A flash of gratified pride mounted to the managerial face,followedby a look of agonised doubt as he evidently reflected that perhaps the General had sot paid for the box; ihe pulled a eard out of his pocket, and scribbling a line on it, told the boy to take it to the box-office, and bring back an answer. The , boy rushed off, his head full of the General, and returned in a few minutes with the same card, which he handed to the manager. A ghastly look crossed his face as he read it, and ' without a word handed it to me. The first line read in the rather shaky managerial caligraphy, ' Did pen. Grant pay for his box?' while underneath appeared, 'No, but my son Fred did. U. S. Grant.' The boy had taken it to the box tasked of the box-office."

RAILWAY COLLISON AT RINDLEY JUNCLION.--COn. siderable damage to the rolling stock and permanent way was causPd by an accident on the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway on Tuesday night. Whilst a Normanton goods train was crossing the line at Hindley Junction a coal train from Wigan came up, and the driver of the pilot engine, failing to notice that the signals were against them, con. tinned pushing the coal train, causing it to run into the luggage train. several waggons were smashed and thrown off the metals. The luggage driver, not noticing what had happened, continued on his way and drew the oyerthrcwn waggons along the permanent way, ploughing it up for nearly 200 yards. Both lines were completely blocked for some time, the Manchester and Liverpool passengers suffer- ing great inconvenience and delay. The through traffic was worked by other routes, but the local passengers had to wait until the debris was cleared away. FIFTY POUNDS FOIL SELLING A PINT OF BEER.—AI Tyne. mouth Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, James Clark was charged with selling a pint of beer without a license. The defendant had supplied a woman with it, and the magis- trates said they were perfectly satisfied the charge bad been proved. They inflicted a fine of a() and costs, owing to his having been previously fined a similar amount for a like offence. Notice of appeal was given on behalf of the defen- dant.

Sir Henry Lopez took his seat on Wednesday morning in the Court of Appeal as a Lord Justice of Appeal, having, oa the retirement of Lord Justice Baggallav, been elevated from the position of a puisne judge of the High Court. Portion of the premises occupied by the Protector Lamp and Lighting Company, at Monton, near Eccles, was des- troyed by fire early on Wednesday morning. The damage, which amourts to about £7,000, is covered by in- euranee.

_ REVOLTING SCENE Al' IN EXECITTION.—Again there has been a revolting scene at an execution. At Norwich Gaol, on Monday, a man who weighed fifteen stone had to be hanged, and Berry, the executioner, allowed a drop of six feet. To the horror of the onlookers. DO soon.r had the trap door fallen and the victim disappear d that the rope re- / bounded, and it was found that the man had been decapita ted as completelY as though he had been placed under the guillotine. The convict, in addition to heir)g a heavy man, had an exceptionally thin vertpbra. and an ignorant execu- tioner could not be expected to necks due allowance for these facts in determining the length and thickness of the rope. But some means ought to be found to prevent oc- currences so repugnant, which must, it is to be feared, recur until the executioner receives more scientific guid- ance.

NORTH WICH ELECTION CAMPAIGN. - MEETING AT RUNCORN.- Mr. J. T. Brunner's election campaign extending over a period of four months was :brought to an ap- propriate and successful conclusion atßuncorn -on Saturday evening by a. torchlight procession and a mass meeting of working-men. In order to dish the Liberals the Tories had obtained control over the Public Hall for several nights, but the party were enabled through the kindness of Mr. Waldron ,to make use of the Theatre Royal, and an admirable meeting-place it proved. The procession formed at the Highlanda, the residence of Mr. It. Shaw, chairman of the Election Committee for the division, shortly after six o'clock, and wended its way down Green- way-road and through the principal streets of the town. Distributed through the ranks of the several hundred persons who look part were about seventy torches, and the area, with the Mill Brow Brass Band playintiand the lights gleaming, was very picturesque.. i In a prominent position was Mr. Brunner, acpbmpanied by Mrs Shaw, while Mr. Shaw escorted Mrs Brunner. Mr. James Handley, J.P., Captain Brunner, and other prominent Liberals also walked. At various points along the route, cheers for Mr. Brunner arose, and when passing Public Hall-street, where the Tories were just arriv- ing for their meeting, a perfect shout of triumph , went up from the processionists and the assembled sympathisers. The demonstration would have been more general but hundreds of earnest Liberals, anxious toi secure good seats, were in the Theatre before haff-past six, and at seven the building was crowded to excess.. Prior to the commencement of the proceedings, the popular refrain "Brunner and -victory " was sung 'with great heartiness, and cheers were given for the leaders of the party whose names adorned the front of the circle. There were calls for a speech from Mr. B. Kniveton, and that gentleman in a few sentences rgferred to the noble battles Mr. Latham had fought for 'Liberalism in Cheshire, and proposed that a resolution cipressing the bestvrishes for his success in Crewe be forwar- ded. Mi. J. R. FRITH seconded the motion, which was carried by three hearty cheers for the old champion ofthe cause. The arrival of Mr. Brun- ner and his party was greeted with prolonged and enthusiastic cheering, the audience rising to their feet en Inane and waving hats and handkerchiefs. A round of 'cheering was given for Mrs. Brunncr, who bowed her acknowledgments. Mr.-James Handley, J.P., presided, and. he was supported on the plat- form by a numerous array of ladies and gentlemen: In a speech cakftlated to maintain-the en,thusiasm of the meeting, ' HANDLEY observed thet the time for tithing was almost over, and the tiiae to act bad arrived. He felt con- fident he could rely Olin' that large assembly to do their duty on nada', next, and return Mr. Brunner by a !riam- phant majoetty. (Cheers.) Urlion wart serensith. They bed been uniteitio fat, and he hoped they'Would maintain that union through the length of Mr. Brunneeti lifetime, that they would have him to represent them. (Cheers.) Their opponent had given it as a reason why be should be re- turned to Parliament that there was do representative of salt. (Laughter.) He was glad to tell them that that ar- gument was now taken away for Mr. Cobbett, a Liberal, lead been returned for Broftwich that day. (Loud cheers.) He congratulated their Liberal friends in the neighbouring divi- sion of Eddisburelpon the gallant .fight they bad made. (Cheers.; Had.Nfrniwell been a little longer in the con- stituency, and better known, he was confident ha would have secured a triumphant victory. However there was hope for the next occasion. (Cheers.) Mr. BRUNNER, on rising, was greeted with an ovation. He declared himself a follower of the best man that' trod the boards of the theatre of politics in this country—(lwed cheers)—and said it was because he had been and was a follower of that great man that it was their bounden duty to poll in his favout on Tuesday next. (Cheers.) He meant to work for the women and children as well as the men. (Hear, hear.) He was in loving sympathy with the heroic efforts lately made to deal with social sores, and should earnestly support all measures directed towards the protection of the daughters of the poor and the purity of their homes. (Cheers.) Mr. Brunner dealt with the various points in his address, enunciating hie 'views upon salmi. dences in the salt "district; free trade, the reform 'of pros cedars in the House of Commons, the land laws, taxation, and free education, which have previously been repotted in the Examiner. Ao to the empire, be was proud of the gal- lantry and pinch that bail maintained it, as any Englishman amongst them, but he did not want England to appear before, the nations of the world'as a determined bully that had nb consideration for the feelings of others. (Hear, heart and cheers.) International arbitration, Lord Salisbury had said, absolhtelv stank in die nostrils of, England. ("Shame.") Those that maintained that opinion should have from hien (Mr. Brunner) this tj*mest pity, and contempt. (Cheers.) For 20 years he bad been, an& should continue to be, an ardent follower of him vrtacr more than any other living states- man bad earned the gratitude and affection of the people. (Cheers.) The " Pilot of the state" was here heartily sung. Mr. T. SNAPS, of Liverpool, moved " That this meeting of the electors of Runcorn polling district congratulatesthe Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone—(cheers)—Lord Hartington (cheers)—Mr. Bright—(cheers)—and Mr. Chamberlain— (prolonged cheers)—and the other leaders of the Liberal , party on their triumphant return—(cheers)—and pledgee itself to use all legitimate efforts to return Mr. Brunner— (loud cheers)—as member for Northerich Division on Tues- day next." ("Three cheers for poor Childers.") Mr: Snape, who bad a most flattering reception, delivered a speech in support of Mr. Brunner, which frequently elicited the utmost enthusiasm. He marvelled that working men should join the Tory party, who gulped at reform hat as people took a gulp of unpleasant physic. (Loud laughter.) _ Mr. JEPSON seconded the resolution, and gave three ex- cellent reasons why they should support Mr. Brunner. - Mr. J. SEWARD, of Liverpool, made a speech in support, in which he contrasted the policy of the Tory party with- the policy of the Liberal party, pointing out how the former had always been the upholders of class privileges. ' The resolution was carried unanimously. The Rev. W. GELLEY, of Northwich, moved "That this meeting recognises with thankfulness the great pro. geese this country has made under Liberal administration, and urges the leaders of the Liberal party to continue their self-sacrificing efforts to promote the commercial, Board, , and religious welfare of the nation." (Heir. hear.) Re made sarcastic reference to the utterances of Mr. Vordin, and to his parson advocate from Runcorn—(" Three groans for Preston ")—and claimed that the Liberal party had been associated with all the great reforms of the past flit! years. (Cheers.) Mr. Robert Soaw, who was received with ringing cheers, seconded the resolution and said he would read one clause from Mr. Verlin's address to show them the utter nonsense as well as the incompetency of the man to deal with what he supposed to be a wrong. "I will," he said, "support any statesmanlike measure which will dispense with the neoes- city of the presence of a registrar at marriages in Noncon- formist places of worship.' What grand language that was. (Laughter.) Statesmanlike measure! (Laughter.) Why ' if they went into one of the schools a boy eight years old would say strike out the clause requiring the registrar's presence. There was a statesmanlike measure. (Laugh. ter.) If they would carefully read that address they would see that whoever conceived it had no conception of either the wrongs under which we suffered or the way in which to repair them. (Hear, hear.) We did not want wrongs remedying in the way the Conservatives had done in the past. If they took away the regiatrar from the Nonconfor- mist marriages they would put something in his place that would make it as distasteful as it was now. (Cheers.) Mr. Shaw again referred to Free Education and the Runcorn wages question, and three groans were given for " Wigg " At the conclusion of his speech Mr. Shaw was given quite an ovation. Mr. T. E. Ellie, of Northwich, supported the resolution in an excellent address. The motion was carried unanimously. In proposing a vote of thanks to the chairman, Mr. Brunner said if the liquor traffic were curtailed they would not stop fun. They would keep open the houses of enter- tainment. Do net let anybody persuade them that the t Liberals were " kill joys," for they were not. ) The vote was carried by acclamation, and Mr. Handlsv, 0 having briefly responded, the proceedings concluded by the 0 singing of the national anthem. 4

RIOTING AT NORTHWICH.

, been formed as the "salt district.''' thriorrunafely ekrlv in the campaign personalities were introduced, and an at- tempt WRS made to injure Mr. Brunner by the argument that his works were the cause of the depression of tbe chemical trade, and the low rate of wages in Runcorn. and were also an injury to the salt trade. These statements were refuted only to be repeated more positively, but al- most upon the eve of the election, Mr. Brunner retorted with crushing effect by producing a letter written by Messrs. Verdin, the contents of which will be fresh in the memory of our readers. Mr. Shaw also made several admirable speeches upon the wage question. He showed that the workmen were not receiving that remuneration to which their labour entitled them, and that in fact they were much worse paid than their brethren "across the river," who per- formed similar work under similar circumstances. These utterances were believed to have gained many " chemic men" to Mr. Brunner's standard, and the Liberal outlook was bright and hopeful to the last. The Tories also ex- pressed themselves confident of a good majority; how far their expectations were justified the result showe. Not- withstanding the manifesto of Mr. Parnell, the Irish electors of the division, or at least the majority of them both in Runcorn and Northwich, gave their support to Mr. Brun- ner, whose expressions of opinion upon Horne Rule,and re- ligions education were clear and explicit. Proceedings of a most regrettable nature occurred at Northwich. Polling proceeded steadily and quietly until about dusk, when the narrow and crooked streets in the neighbourhood of the Market-hall became thronged with some thousands of people, and between six and seven o'clock a disturbance of a very serious character took place in Mar- ket-street. A man, carrying a big loaf on his head, was passing the Conservative committee-room, when some per- sons in the surging crowd, out of pure mischief, pushed him in the doorway. Several other men stumbled with him, and, fearing an inrush, the occupants of the room took prompt steps to eject the intruaers. In this, however, they were unsuccessful, as the crowd pressed forward, and in a few minutes filled the room. With the aid of some gentle- men from the Liberal committee-room, they were eventually persuaded to withdraw, but on getting outside they as- sumed a menacing attitude, and some eight or nine police- men, under Colonel Hammersley, the chief constable lined the parapet in front of els building. The fury of the mob, however, increased, and at last the premises were stormed with stones and brickbats, which were burled through the large plate-glass window of Mr. Hughes' sale room (used as the committee-room). The police, who exhibited marvel- lous forbearanre, stood their ground without taking any strong measures to quiet the disturbance. A number of young fellows and women continued throwing stone, until at length there was not an inch of glass left in the frame- work. The doors were battered down, each act of dest.mc- tion being hailed with cheers. This portion of the building having been completely wrecked, the infuriated mob turned its attention to the windows in Mr. Hughes' office, which they elso demolished. As the excitement increased, Mr. Kay, the senior magistrate of the district, after consultation with Colonel ilamersley, Chief Conetable, read the Riot Act from the 'Steps of the Market Hall. This failing to produce the de- sired effect, the police, augmented by reserves, charged the Crowd with drawn trnucheons. Col. Hamersley having pre- viously given instructions not to touch persons fri ndly to them. 'Toe scene which followed was one of the wildest excitement. The constables dashed into the bowling throng, and letting out right and left with staves, a large number of persons were struck, some with considerable violence. Market-street was speedily cleared, but the crowd, which congregated in neighbouring streets, retalia- ted by hurling stones at the officers. Constable Wood, for- merly of Middlewich, was violently struck on the back of the bead, and for a time incapacitated. Constaale Jackson, of Stockport, also sustained a terrific blow' behind the ear, which completely stunned , him. Other officers were injured, but less seriously. Stones were thrown at the Market-hall windows and as Jas. Hayes, of Witton, was leaving the hall, he was struck on the top of the head with a huge stone and fell senseless. He was laid on a stall in the hall, where he was attended to by Dr. Morton ; he eventually rallied, and was able to pro- ceed home with assistance. The attitude of the people still being threatening, Col. Hameraley, after further consultation with Mr. Kay, tele- graphed for reinforcements from various parts of the county, and requested the military authorities at Chester to have soldiers in readiness to proceed to the assistance of the police at a moment's notice. The poll closed at eight, and the sealed ballot boxes were conveyed to the Sessions House, Leicester-street, where the votes were to be counted. After this the excitement was considerably allayed, and meet of the, police were marched to the police station amid the jeers of the crowd, one officer being struck on the head by a stone in Crown-street. The streets continued in an excited state, and some exuberant politicians harangued the crowd at various points. At nine o'clock Mr. Brunner arrived in town and walked to the Ses- sions House, escorted by a cheering throng. In Leicester- street he mounted a cab and said : There has been sorne talk of your having made up your minds to have a row. I don't believe anything of the sort. (Cheers.) I want you to back me to keep up a good name for Northwich. (Cheers.) Very well, lam satisfied with you. (Cheers.) At Winsford, Barnton, Middlewich, 'Marston, dm., the pro- ceedings passed cff without any serious incidents, but par- tisanship was shown by throwing paper bags containing red raddle, blue povider, flour, &o, but good humour pre- vailed all round.

The election of a member of Parliament to represent the Northwich Division of Cheshire took place on Tuesday. By the Act of Redistribution this constituency was carved out of the Mid-Cbee6ire Division, which for an unbroken period of about 30 years was represented by two Conservative members. It contains a population of nearly 60,000, and has a total electorate of 10,577, the principal towns in- cluded within its boundaries being Northwicb, Runcorn, Wiosford, and Middlewich. Many stiff battles between the champions of Liberalism and Toryism have been fought in the old division, but in severity and strong excitement aroused none have paralleled the contest that concluded on Tuesday night. By a majority of 30 votes, Mr. John Tom- linson Brunner, of Winnington Old Hall, was selected as the Liberal candidate by the 300 " over Mr. Robert Verdiu, chief of the firm of Messrs. Verdin and Sons, salt manu- facturers, of 7i,)rthwich ; and the partisan feeling ran Sc) high, thAt there was a fear at one time that there would be a split in the Liberal c imp. A few weeks passed, and then the announcement was made that Mr. William Henry Vet. din, brother to the would-be Liberal representative, was to come forward in the Conservative interest. By numerous meeting., extending over a period of the past four months, Mr. Brunner made the acquaintance of the electors; the Liberal ranks closed up ; and they presented a united front to their opponents. Mr. Brunner avowed himself a Liberal of advanced views and earnest purpose; but his opponent at the outset basid his chief claim upon the people on the fact that he was a salt proprietor, that salt ought to be represented, and that the constituency had
