"Gentlemen, I regreCto have to say to foil some words that are not pleasant for me to utter, and fear it will not be pleasant for yon'tontear. r" very much regret that this election 'bee been darkened by conduct which none of us look back upon with pleasure. (Hear, hear.) But let me tell you;and I tell you with confidence, I don't b.lieve that that has been the work of Liberals. (Cheers.) Gentlemen, some 24 hours ago my heart was gladdened by the news that came from Crewe. (Cheers.) I ask your permission to convey to our old friend George William Latham a hearty message of congratulation. (Cheers.) Gentlemen, I am the s.,cond Liberal county member for Cheshire—(cheers)—and I heartily trust that the next week will add several more to that number. (Cheers.) Now, gentlemen, I trust that you consider that my con- duct during this election has been such as will entitle me to say that I have given just offence to no man— (cheers)—that I hold myself justly entitled to look forward to retain the friendship of every man, woman, and child in the constituency. (Cheers.) Now we are going to be neighbours for many a day, and I can afford now to say a hearty good-night to you. (Loud cheers.) Mr. R. SHAW, of Runcorn, addressed a few words to the , erowd, asking them to show their appreciation of Mr. Brunner by going home in peace, and resting satisfied that they bad done their duty. (Cheers.) The people then dispersed. Mrs. Brunner, who was wait- ing at Mr. Thomas's, was heartily congratulated on the victory by a large circle of friends.

The Liberal organisation in the division was admirable, and great credit is due to Mr. W. Handley, the registration agent for his skilful and energetic labour. Mr. Brunner, prior to the election, paid a compliment to Mr. Handley for his talent and labour. Mr. James Handley, J.P., and Mr. Thomas Ehndlev have taken an important part in the campaign, and the labours of Mr. Fl'toiler, Mr. J. R. Frith, Mr. B. Kniveton, and others are deserving of the fullest acknowlEdgement.
KNUfSFuRD ELECTION.

Tbe election of a member of Parliament for the Knats• ford Division of Cheshire took place on Thursday, and re- suited in the return of the Tory candidate. The narrow majority given in favour of the Conservative candidate in the Eddisbury Division, supported and aided as he was by local influences of the most powerful kind, were considered by the Liberals of the division as encouraging. Mr. J. E. ' Barlow, it was conceded, entered upon the contest in the face of a most powerful opponent and in view of great ob- stacles. For generations the Egertous of Tatton had held the representation of this portion of Cheshire in tkeir hands, and never once had a Liberal succeeded in wresting it from them:- But recent contests had shown that Liberalism, al- though not lii the ascendant, was in increasing force in the constituency; and when, by the beneficent operations of the Franchise Act, electoral power was conferred upon a vast mambo of the inhabitants whose voices bad hitherto been unheard at thepol ling booths, it was hoped that the efforts of the Liberal party would at length be crowned with success. Upon the task of opposing a member of the house Of Tatton Mr. Barlow entered with a light heart. It said something for the progress of Liberalism in Cheshire that 'a MOst enthusiastic Liberal demonstration could be held in Kautsford itself, while in other portions of the divi- sion largely-attended Liberal meetings have received the candidate of the party with acclamation and have passed, in many easea unanimously, resolutions favourable to his candidature. A young man, Mr. Barlow is an excellent 'platform speaker. Every influence of the Tory party, ter- titorial and eocleliatatical, has been arrayed against him, and no stone has tighu left unturned to prevent him from securing the seat. The division is a long and straggling one, extending from the borders of the county at Warring- ton, and Daresbury in the west to Styal in the east, and going southward to Whaley Bridge on the borders of Derby- shire. The electoral roll contains the names of 9,314 elec- tors, who are distributed as follows :—Adlington, 272; Alderley, 587; Allostocic, 375; Aston-bv-Budworth, 144 ; 801 l ington, 909; Daresbury, 467; Disley, 679 ' • Grappenhall, 597; Holmes Chapel. 49i; Knutsford. 9,53; Lostock Gralam, 401 ; Mobberley, 303; Poynton-with-Worth, 416; Prest- bury, 237; Rainow, 304; Siddington, 376; Whaley Bridge,.393; Whitley, 224; and Wilmslow, 1,199. ' There were twenty-tour polling places in the division, the centre of which is Knumford. The majority of the voters walked, many of them considerable distances, to the poll, but con- veyances were used by both parties. So far as could be as,- certained, the polling was conducted without the slightest disorder or disturbance. In the course of the day Mr. B. Armitage, M.P., and Mr. J. T. Brunner, newly-elected member for the Northwich Division, voted at the Knutsford polling station. The polling station for the Daresbury district was at the Board Schools, Daresbury, where the electors for Acton Grange, Datesbury, Hatton, Keekwick, Mciore;'' Newton-by- Daresbury, Preston-on-the-Hill, Stretton, Walton Inferior, Walton Superior, and Hyde John, polled. Very little ex- citement was occasioned. ' The Conservatives had a large number of carriages lent for the occasion, three of which had been placed at their divosal by bit. Gilbert Greenall, M.P. The Liberals were conspicuously short of vehicles, only two or three having been lent. Mr. Aston solicitor, of Frod- ' sham, was the presiding officer, and the personation agents ' Messrs. T. Houghton (for the Conservatives) and Luke Jones (for the Liberals). Electors were asked to " Vote for ' Egerton and Church and State," while large pesters here and there adorned the walls, requesting the electors to " Vote for Barlow, the farmers' friend, and State mainten. ance of roads, improved dwellings for the working classes, and cheap food and plenty of money to buy it with." ' The voting at Crrappenhall proceeded quietly after eleven ' o'clock, up to which time the Conservatives claimed to have polled 171 against 41 of /he-Liberals. The polling station ' for the Grappenhall district, which includes the townships ' of Appleton. Cirappenhall, and Latchford, was the Church schools, the presidic:g officer being Mr. Way, of Chester, the poll clerk Mr. Hamilton, and the personation agents Messrs. Gerrard (Liberal) and John Bolton (Conservative.) There was very little excitement in the village, and the proceed-
ins throughout the day were good-humoured. The count- ing of the votes took place on Friday, and the poll was declared at five minutes to two, with the following re, salt.

div.head: POLL AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THE POLL AT RUNCORN.

As the largest town in the conetituency, Runcorn played a prominent part in the election. Within its boundaries reside one-third of the total electorate, and neither can.li- date, so far as speaking was concerned, neglected the in- habitants. But thesbusy little port, from its past history, and the display of the political proclivities of the people during the past four months, was with good reason re- garded as Mr. Brunner's stronghold, and a poll of nearly two to one is estimated as the strength of the parties. The arrangements for taking the poll were very convenient and complete. There were two polling stations, one being the Market Hall and the other Mr. Cooper's sailrooni, in Station- road. The residents in Runcorn North, numbering 2.173, -voted at the Market Hall, where there were were four booths, and the 913 voters in the South at the Ballroom, where there were two booths. fhe presiding officers were Messrs. F. A. Lake, W. D. Jolliffe, John Ashton, and A. Linaker, of Runcorn; Raymond Harris and W. Peers, of Chester; and the names of their clerks Messrs. W. Pewnall, Jun., W. Brooks, W. Sutton, Joseph Cunnah, T. C. Hughes, and Peters. Messrs. F. A. Smith, R. Wright, W. Mellor, H. A. Hankinson, A. Riley, E. Marwood, W. Fisher, W. Littler, J. D. Jones, James Collier, John Ball, F. Johnson, and C. Williams were personation agents. The weather was highly favourable for the occasion, and the voters arrived in a steady stream all day, there being at no period of the polling what might be called a "great rush." Both parties had committee rooms in close proximity to the booths, and were hard at work all day. On neither side were the vehicles in use numerous, but in this respect the Tories had the advantage. Party favours were extensively worn, and the ladies declared their partisanship in bright colours of red and yellow, their presence adding much to the animated scene. With the exception of Holy Trinity School, the schools were closed, and it was fine fun to the youngsters to be permitted to congregate in the street and hoot and cheer as they desired without interference. There was, however, a complete absence ef excitement until somewhat late in the afternoon, when Mr. Verdin drove iota the town, accompanied by his brother, Mr. Joseph Verdin, The cheers that greeted his arrival were almost unheard amid the groans and hooting that ascended from the assem- bled hundreds, and the carriage moved onwards. About the same time Mr. Brunner had arrived at the railway station, land aczamoanied by Mr. James Handley, JP., and Mr. R. I Shaw, entered an open conveyance. Amid great cheering the crowd unyoked the horses, ropes were attached to the conveyance, and it was rapidly drawn through the town to the Market Hall. Cheers arose on every hand, ladies showered down flowers upon him from the windows as he passed, and his progress was one of triumph. Near the "big lamp" Mr. Shaw delivered a brief address to those present, and then Mr. Brunner said—l knew well seventeen years ago that Cheshire was Liberal—(cheers)and this day's work, believe me, is going to show that we were right (Cheers.) Seventeen years ago we worked for Mr. Warren. (Cheers.) Since then for whom have we worked? (Cheers.) We have worked for Mr. Latham, and now at last Mr. Latham is triumphant. (Loud cheers.) We can say and say, with a glad • heart, "Cheshire at last is free." (Pro- longed cheering.) Amid an enthusiastic acclaim of voices, Mr. John Simpson came forward and greeted the candidate. Towards dusk the streets became more crowded, and an elector proceeded through the streets with a large loaf fixed upon a pole. Opposite the Con- servative committee rooms he stopped, and as there was some apprehension of a disturbance the police relieved the man of his burden. Later, a crowd of young men and youths having obtained some long wooden rails, stretched themselves across the thoroughfare, and then rushed along with an excited crowd at their heels. Many persona had narrow eitcapes of being kuooked down and trampled upon, and a small disturbance might easily have developed into a riot. Sergeant Whalley, of Frodeham, formerly of Runcorn, went to the wild fellows, and after quietly reasoning they gave bins the rails, and as he marched off with them npon his shoulder, "three cheers for Whalley " were heartily given. The poll closed at eight o'clock, and the ballot boxes having been sealed were conveyed to Northwich where the counting took place. Waiting for the result from about ten o'clock, several hundred Liberals ia Bethesda Lecture Hall had an impromptu entertainment, and thoroughly enjoyed themselves. About four hundred hundred waited in Fountain-equare, and when the result was made known about one o'clock, a deafening cheer arose and was continued for some minutes. Result:— Brunner (L) 5,023 Verdin (C)

Lord Randolph Churchill has intimated to a friend that it is his intention to stand again for Birmiorham. A t..TEAMIHt SUNK BY COLLISION.—The screw steamer Wakefield, of Grimsby, was run down on Monday night in the Humber, by the screw steamer Chester, also of Grimsby. Th

le Wakefield sank quickly. All hands but one were saved, the stewardess being drowned. Both ships belong to the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire • Railway Com- pany. RAILWAY COLLISION.-0/1 Friday morning, about six o'clock, a collision occurred between two goods trains on the South-Eastern Railway. A down goods train had left the rails near Charlton Junction. and an up goods train dashed into it, smashing several trucks. The attendants were severely shaken, and the lines were blocked for some hours.

BAD CASE OF BOICOTTIN6.—The lighthouse keepers on the Fastnet Rock are in a serious position. The contractor for supplying the keepers with stores lass been boycotted, and his employes refuse to take out food to the lighthouse. The gunboat Britomart has proceeded from Queenstown to render assistance, but it is doubtful if she can communicate until the gale moderates. DEATH OF A CANDIDATE.—CoIoneI Trefusis, C. 8., the Conservative candidate for the South Molton Division of Devonshire, died on Thursday night. The polling for. the division took place on Thursday, and the declaration of the result was expected yesterday. The deceased officer corn- minded the Scots Guards in the recent operations at Souakim. He was the son of the nineteenth Baron Clinton, arid was married to Lady Mary, daughter of the fifth Duke of Buccleuch. LORD HARTINCiTON AT MANSFIELD.—The Marquls of Hartington, speaking at Mansfield, on Friday afternoon, contended that from the nature of the Liberal party there must be a difference of opinion amongst them. With refer- ence to Fair Trade, he urged that the Reyal Commission for inquiry into trade could not afford any practical remedy for the present depression. As to the results of the elecilan, be said the time had not arrived to enable them to make an accurate estimate. The Conservative successes in the boioughs he attributed partly to division among the Liberals and to the support of the Irish party. TERRIFIC GALE.—A Ramsey (Isle of Man) correspondent telegraphs: A terrific southerly gale bas DrPvailel here since eight o'clock on Thursday night. Considerable dam- age has been done to property. The smack Ethel. of Ram- sey, was driven ashore, but the crew are safe. An Edinburgh correspondent says :—A terrible • gale from the west has swept over Scotland during the past twelve hours, doing great damage to shipping and property of every description. In the country districts stacks of hay have been scattered to the winds, and in Edinburgh several vehicles bave been blown over in the streets. Same damage has also been done to the Exhibition. Much anxiety is felt as te shipping disasters.

RECRUITERS AND RECRUITS. Fir,—The poor untutored private soldier may not know that the life he leads is a profession, but not so with the Re- cruiting Sergeant; he knows and feels proud in the know- ledge that the calling he follows is a profession, and a noble one; for surely 'tis true nobleness that impels a man for his country's rights to meet her fees on the field of battle. My reasons for particularizing the recruiter are that he is generally an old and tried soldier, having his breast deco- rated with the medals; one whose knowledge and expeti- ence on all military matters are exc-ptional ; one having had abundant opportunities of making himself acquainted with everything in connection with a soldier's life. Secondly, that he has a great many more responsibilities than the pub- ' lic in general are aware of, though I'll only instance one, the moral one. Does he feel conscious of having conscien- tiously advised or disadvised every recruit offering himself to him for enrolment in the army? For the conscientious recruiter will be most careful while picturing the advan- tages of the army to his recruit to, at the same time, I minutely impress on his memory its counterparts, such as those resulting from mis-behaviour in all its various and multitudinous forms. When you behold the Recruiting Sergeant neatly attired, his hair carefully brushed, and his boots exquisitely polished, along with his gold or silver. headed cane, you are apt to suppose that the life he leads is an easy it not a jolly one; but on closely scrutinizing it you'll perceive that it, too, has its spice of bitterness. He is very often an object of ridicule, receiving unmeiited showers of abusive language from the mothers and sisters of youths who have voluntarily offered themselves to him. Though there are hundreds of youths entering the army whose absence will be lamentably missed by the beloved ones at home, yet there are thousands of others who could claim neither kindred nor home, and with what mingled feelings of gratitude and respect they look back upon that day of long age, as they were wandering homeless through the streets of our large towns in possession of nothing but the direst destitution ; their limbs scarcely covered, and their stomachs suffering from inanition, when for the first titan, perhaps, they came face to face with the Recruiting Sergeant, who in a manner made them what they now are— men chosen for their punctuality, soberness, and good be- haviour to fill places of responsib litv and trust that any roan might be proud of. I will herein instance a meeting that took place (of which I was art eye witness) between a warrant officer and the sergeant who enlisted him. "Tie now, sir, 14 (to me very short) years since I was your re- cruit, since which time I have sees many strange countries and passed through many strange scenes, but through all I still remembered your advice and strictly adhered to it, to which in a measure I ascribe and owe my present position. I am still but a young man, and am ever aspiring to soar higher and higher till I reach the rank of him whose achievements you were so fond of relating." The Recruiting Sergeant in filling up the gaps in the army, which must necessarily be, is performing a doubly important duty to his sovereign and country; for what would have become of our vast Indian Empire if the Re- cruiting Sergeant had not busied himself, and actively too, in sending our warriors to its relief ? It had long ago passed from us, and believe me, that if ever such a catas- trophe occurs it will be the setting of England's star of greatness and grandness. The poor soldier who faces death at the command of his superior belongs to that profession wherein every single member has voluntarily and solemnly sworn that be will defend to the last drop of his blood his Queen and country from all enemies, and surely, none will deny that to riek one's life for one's country's welfare is a noble thing.—Yours, WILLIAM CAVANEY.

THE GENERAL ELECTION. A GLIMPSE INTO THE FUTURE.

The following, which appeared in a Manchester paper before the Elections, has been posted on the walls throughout Warrington :- 1. At November election, in 1885, in round num- bers, 300 Liberals, 300 Conservatives, and 100 Nationalists returned (by Irish vote in the three kingdoms). Her Majesty requested Lord Salisbury to continue in office. Having 100 Nationalists as his majority, he consented. 2. Legislation accomplished : (a) Procedure: Not touched, majority did not re- quire it. (b) Land Legislation: None attempted, because I Ireland was satisfied, and Great Britain could I wait.

(c) State Church: Secure and victorious, since majority- desired it. N.8.---Dissenters gloomy and ominously desperate (in Scotland). (d) Trade: Free Trade rigime revised; war of tar- iffs begun with America, France, Germany, and Spain; rise in the price of bread. (e) Ireland: Lord Lieutenancy abolished;. Parlia- ment in Dublin; Republic.; Mr. Parnell elected first president; return of Irish Americans, &o:; things getting warm; coast opposite Great Britain rapidly arming; 3. Foreign Policy, European conflagration; Ser- via defeated by Bulgaria; Austria to the rescue; Bulgaria almost annihilated; Russia enters the arena; ngland attempts to " arbitnite ; "Hands off ; " War between Austria and Russia; threats of Germany disregarded ; Germany attacks Rus- sia ; England assists Austria With fleet;: Italy and France maintain armed neutrality. 4. Domestic policy. Royal Commission conclu- ded Tabours ; divided, opinions in various parts of report; foreign luxuries taxed; English exports taxed more heavily; trade. gone, wages sink, prices rise, pauperism and/ crime on the increase; high population " boycotted " in England, and returning to Ireland to famine and despair; West Coast of Great Britain put in a state of complete defence against Ireland; stagnation of comnaerce ; Irish cruisers attacking British merchantmen; • Radicals discontented; Tories dismayed. 5 .'What caused In 1885 the. Reties and Par- nellites united to swamp the Liberals; Irish reaped benefit ; the Tory was a cat's paw of the Hibermans, and was drawn at the cart's tail of rebellion in cam- sequence, then discarded. (b) By Conservatives and Whigs believing the Radicals when they. said the- Church was outside party politics. (e) By both Liberals and. Conservatives' being patriotic, and, seeing the issue, making al strong Liberal majority in the House of Commons, which would hate avoided the hatred, ruin, rebellion, and break-up of the Empire above pourtrayed.. ASSAULT. —James Tarpey, of Thirtonwoad, was sum- mored at the Newton Petty seesions, on Satarday, for as- siulting William Jones at Bortonwood, on the 6th ult. The complainant, who was employed as a fireman at Collins Green Colliery, stated that he was stanuing in the okce when the defendant came past, and without the slightest warning struck him a" swinging blow " on the mouth. The defendant had been previously employed on the night shift, and complainant had suspended !Ain far neglect of work until he saw the manager about it. The Bench in- flicted a fine of 59 and costs.

N years of re, lodging at 61, Ormskirk-street, St. Helens, and employed as a pattern maker, was journey- ing to Ilackbrook on the seven ()Mock tram-car from St. Helens to Hap:hick. Some brandy was administered to him, and a doc or was sent for, but the ploy man died in about five minutes. Dr. Masson has cer- tified that he died front heart disease.

the reform necessary for the further amelioration of the condition of the people and the development of a higher civilization. I refer to the question of Peace and War. Hitherto the power to engage in war has been vested in our rulers, a power which has been greatly abused and which has entailed enormous sacrifices of blood and treasure upon the people. For, although they have been denied a voice in the making of wars, it is they who have been called upon to provide the means to carry them on. But it is not merely when we are actually engaged in war that we are called upon to make these sacrifices, for we find that three- fourths of our annual expenditure is swallowed up in the payment of interest and management of debt for past wars and the preparations for future wars. During the last half century which, with the exception of the Crimean war, has been regarded comparatively as a period of peace, we have been engaged in no less than 65 wars, am) in half that time we have spent on war and interest on debt no less than fourteen hundred million pounds sterling, whereas the total amount expended on the civil seavices during the same period of time has been four hundred million pounds sterling, or one thousand millions more for war than for the civil service, or mole than three-quarters of the total expenditure. But this is only one phase of the cost of war. Look at the whole continent of Europe, and what do we dud? That there are 12 millions of men trained to army, drawn from the peaceful pursuits of productive industry, to be main- tained for the purpose of upholding a system of militatvism which costs annually, including interests on debts, 650 mil- lion pounds sterling. Think of it! An automat almost equal in value to the whole of the foreign trade of Great Britain.

A great deal has recently been said about the-depression In trade, and working-men have been told by those who knew better, but who are anything and everything, if by any means they can succeed in snatching a few emtra, votes for their party, that this depression is owing to Free Trade and for this purpose they are offered a bribe in the form of a reimposition of duties en all goods imported into the coun- try, in order, forsooth, to protect them against foreign com- petition. Let those who have been led to waver in their faith in our commercial policy read the following paragraph from a speech delivered by the present (nominal) leader of the Conservative party, the Marquis of Salisbury, before the Manchester Chamber if Commerce a few years ago. Referring to these duties, he said : " The real cause of this increase of protective duties is the establishment of these gigantic military forces, which are increasing every year, in everyone of the larger coun- tries of this hemisphere, which constitute a permanent drain! on the forces of industry, a permanent danger to the inter- ests of commerce, and which impose upon the Governments which feel themselves bound—and if one Government does it, all have to do it—in order to maintain their forces, the necessity of finding money in some way that shall not gall too heavily the interests and susceptibilities of their people. Indirect taxation,it is well known, is more readily paid than direct taxation, because its amount is not so easily recog- nised, and it is the necessity of finding the 'sustenance of those vast armaments that forces Governments to have re- course to indirect taxation." I have said More, sir, and I repeat it here, that for once in his life the noble marquis spoke the truth when he gave utterance to that statement. and I say there is no stronger condemnation of the position with regard to Free Trade, which he has now taken up, than is contained in that state- ment. However he matt try to shield himself behind the sophisms, so common amongst those who occupy the same anomalous position as himself, I commend it to the con- sideration of working-men of both parties, for therein they will find the real object of the proposed reimposition of duties, and they will see that it is not Free Trade which is paralyzing the industries of Europe. It is to a great extent this galling yoke of militarism, and Free Trsde tends only to mitigate the evil, for so long as 12 millions of men are taken from the hives of productive industry to he trained for the purpose of destroying the industry of others, and each nation is armed to the teeth, ready to war on its neighbour on the slightest pretext, to devastate their cities, and destroy in every possible way the fruits of their labour, so long may we expect the attention of our legislators to be called away from the urgent needs of remedial legislation at home, for reforms will be delayed, the maintenance of peace difficult, and retrenchment impossible. But how can all this be remedied? Well, hitherto it has been extremely difficult. There has been such a large por- tion of our representatives who have been directly or in- directly interested in the maintenance of this policy of lolly and extravagance, and the governing power has been as ! largely monopolised by the landed aristocracy' who have I also monopelised all the military, civil, and religious emoluments of the State, that they have taken good care ! both in the representative House of Commons, and (especially) in the non-representative House of Lords to fan the flame of national prejudice, to play upon national pride, and to keep alive those false sentiments of national honour, ' which have been productive of so many sanguinary and dis- astrous wars, which have galled so heavily the interests and susceptibilities of the people." But now all this may be altered. This power may now be wrested from those who have lorded over the working classes, posed so loftily as their betters. Never before has "the toe of the peasant ' come so nigh upon the heel of the courtier," and it "galls his kiba," for he sees that ere long he will be hurled from his arrogant prominence ta rub shoulder to shoulder with those whom he has been wont to regard as being made for ' his interest and support. Hence his long and persisteut opposition to the just demands of the people, and hence his ; impudent sycophancy in posing now as the working-man's friead, for having at last yielded to the demands be could no longer resist. Peace should be secured net by indulging in blatant jingoism and a still further augmentation of the already bloated armaments Of Europe, but a permanent and honourable peace, based on a simultaneous reduction of armamems and the settlement of all international disputes by a system of international arbitration instead of war.— RATHBONE. Yours, Ice., 43, Arpley-street, Warrington.
